topics.title: [experiment] BFCL multi-harness DPO recovery: results and remaining work
topics.body:
## TL;DR

The BFCL multi-harness recovery campaign did not reach its goal. We exercised DPO (direct preference optimization) in Levanter, implemented and tested native DPO in MarinSkyRL, and built trace retention, preference curation, and multi-harness collection infrastructure. The extended native DPO run degraded Pi accuracy from 34/123 at initialization to 10/123 after four updates and 0/123 after eight; we stopped it after preserving intermediate evaluations. Harness transfer was partial and large score differences persisted across harnesses. A separate model-merging campaign recovered substantially more measured BFCL-Parity performance than the DPO recipes tested here, with important selection and comparability limits.

## Description

The original objective was to improve function calling from the Grug-67B-A2B Antidoom/RLVR1 step-12 lineage and demonstrate multi-harness robustness: the worst harness should reach at least 70% of the best harness's score. Grug is a mixture-of-experts model with approximately 67 billion total and 2 billion active parameters; Antidoom/RLVR1 identifies its prior de-looping and reinforcement-learning checkpoint lineage. Labels such as `.304` and `.356` are campaign run/artifact identifiers. Training used the 3,518-task BFCL complement, excluding the 123 BFCL-Parity tasks. Offline DPO was used to improve the weak starting policy before attempting further online RL.

BFCL-Parity is Harbor's `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation of the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard. Pi, Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, and Mini-SWE are agent harnesses that provide prompts, tool interfaces, and execution loops around the model. Each evaluation task receives one agent trial; accuracy means passing the task verifier. These tasks require `/app/result.json`, whose existence alone is insufficient for success. The scores below are adaptation-specific solve rates, not standard BFCL leaderboard scores. See the [public evaluation policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9566).

## Hypothesis or Goal

Learn function-calling behavior that transfers across harnesses while preserving task accuracy. The campaign tested whole-trajectory preference training, not the localized token/action objectives proposed in the follow-ups.

## Status

Learning work is stopped. The campaign achieved these infrastructure milestones:

- Levanter DPO produced the `.304` initializer after two additional optimizer updates and a 39-shard HF-format export. This checkpoint descended from an earlier 58-update DPO warm start; it was not trained directly from the original model in two updates. [Export receipt](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/trials/daytona-expanded-training-v304-verified.json).
- Native DPO was [merged into MarinSkyRL in #954](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/954). Pipeline smoke `.356` connected fresh collection, curation, four applied updates, Pi evaluation, and export. Its 64-pair batch contained one newly collected pair; this was not an all-harness fresh-data smoke. Accuracy fell from 28/123 to 7/123. [Optimizer and pipeline receipt](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/trials/final-pipeline-v356-verified.json).
- The collection/curation path retains teacher/student traces, exact tokens and masks where captured, verifier outcomes, task identities, immutable partial batches, and preference provenance. Four harnesses supplied the final training cohort; Pi was the evaluation harness. These components support future datakit mining, but do not yet implement verified same-history local repair pairs. [Infrastructure inventory](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/technical-progress-20261011.md), [pinned campaign code](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl).
- A complete online multi-harness RL optimizer loop was not demonstrated. Collection, native trace capture, rollout configuration, and training components exist; their full on-policy integration remains unverified. Some fixes remain on campaign branches or open PRs.

The final native DPO input contained 1,712 pairs from 633 tasks unseen by the initializer's recorded training lineage. We planned 107 updates at 16 pairs/update, with Pi validation before training and every four updates. Applied updates are verified through 35, with nine completed evaluation panels and a partial update-36 panel. The initializer remained the best evaluated checkpoint. [Collapse analysis](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/dpo-collapse-investigation-20261011.md), [archive/stop receipt](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/trials/final-dpo-forensics-stop-verified.json).

## Results and limits

Levanter's short `.304` continuation improved the measured panel relative to its `.26` warm start: Pi 23/122 to 35/123, Claude Code 15/123 to 29/123, OpenCode 8/123 to 24/123, and Mini-SWE 8/123 to 16/123. The Pi baseline attempted 123 tasks with one infrastructure-ungraded result. These are single panel comparisons, not repeated statistical estimates. Public warm-start receipts: [Pi](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/7c63db4501ba6d3a523db18726d3855cf96b0afb/trials/daytona-reference-parity-v311-2026.10.04.26-pi-verified.json), [Claude Code](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/7c63db4501ba6d3a523db18726d3855cf96b0afb/trials/daytona-reference-parity-v311-2026.10.04.26-claude-code-verified.json), [OpenCode](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/7c63db4501ba6d3a523db18726d3855cf96b0afb/trials/daytona-reference-parity-v311-2026.10.04.26-opencode-verified.json), [Mini-SWE](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/7c63db4501ba6d3a523db18726d3855cf96b0afb/trials/daytona-reference-parity-v311-2026.10.04.26-mini-swe-agent-verified.json).

The earlier `.304` panel scored Pi 35/123 (28.46%), Claude Code 29/123 (23.58%), OpenCode 24/123 (19.51%), and Mini-SWE 16/123 (13.01%). Codex covered only 105/123 tasks and was not a valid canonical panel. The worst valid score was 46% of the best, below the required 70%. These results show harness-dependent performance; they do not isolate a causal training-mixture effect. The later 34/123 native-run baseline is a separate evaluation of the initializer.

The best related published merge, [Shared100](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-NUPA-BFCL-Shared100-2026.10.09/tree/462ad9af071055da39ef4bfea1d4ba2c9429a223), scored 60/123 (48.78%) on BFCL-Parity Pi, versus `.304`'s 35/123. In our experiments, merging recovered more measured performance than the tested DPO recipes. However, BFCL-Parity activation traces informed expert selection in the merge campaign, and the benchmark was reused for model selection. Its score is an optimization result, not a clean held-out or controlled causal comparison with DPO. Parent mixtures and training histories differ, and the merge's Pi score does not establish multi-harness robustness. [Merge campaign](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975).

At native DPO update 8, all 123 tasks lacked the required result file. Successful file-writing demonstrations existed in the preference data. Rejected responses contributed about 7.24 times as many supervised tokens as chosen responses, with extreme tool-syntax repetition. These observations motivate local, bounded training targets. They do not establish the precise gradient mechanism behind the collapse. Independent distributed-update and training-to-serving numerical equivalence remain [deferred verification experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/issues/969), not discovered bugs.

## Links

Datakit is [Marin's data preparation and chat-rendering library](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit). Linked historical reports retain local/internal provenance paths; the public release supports aggregate inspection rather than complete independent replay. Evaluation runtime pins also differ between the DPO and merge campaigns, so their results are separate campaign measurements.

- [Public screened campaign artifacts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/tree/9be5d36578c27140a75caac1e31ecdefb76cff0b): 7,356 files, reports, scripts, configurations, aggregate receipts, model publication verification, and an exclusion manifest. Raw conversations, private DPO datasets, third-party payloads, secrets, and runtime directories are withheld. Public aggregates do not permit independent replay of every private-trace analysis.
- [Best DPO initializer, BFCL-Recovery (`.304`)](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Recovery/tree/850a32627724d274004241dd10f6cb46fd3f6f83): public, 39 BF16 shards, with all uploaded file hashes verified. The model card explains the inherited stale manifest and the scope of provenance checks. It received no updates from the degrading extended run. [Best related published merge and limitations](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-NUPA-BFCL-Shared100-2026.10.09/tree/462ad9af071055da39ef4bfea1d4ba2c9429a223) is a separate model.
- [Pinned MarinSkyRL runtime](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/fa6da4d8c67ed17b3fa69f689d9b444694683f8a), [pinned Harbor runtime](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/tree/436d0c92ed2fbb679438cd750e5fab3328153c31).
- Open follow-ups: [localized online feedback #10043](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043), [datakit single-turn comparison mining and DPO validation #10042](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10042), and [complete online multi-harness RL integration #10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041).

## Decision Log

- Used offline preference learning while baseline task success remained low.
- Moved from Levanter to native MarinSkyRL DPO to exercise the unified trainer and periodic Pi evaluation.
- Stopped the extended run after degradation, preserving intermediate traces for analysis.
- Separated future behavioral interventions from the uncompleted online integration work.

## Conclusion

The performance and harness-robustness objectives remain unmet. The campaign leaves tested DPO plumbing and reusable collection/curation components, with three explicit follow-ups. Closing this issue archives the campaign; it does not certify successful recovery or complete online multi-harness RL.

topics.title: Mine and validate same-history local DPO pairs with datakit
topics.body:
Design, implement, execute, and validate reusable datakit tooling that turns retained agent traces into same-history, single-turn preference examples, then determine whether DPO learns the intended local behavior without degrading task performance. The BFCL campaign already retains traces, preference provenance, task identities, and token masks; verified local-pair extraction remains to be built. [Infrastructure inventory](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/technical-progress-20261011.md).

A bounded bad action is one erroneous tool action or a precisely identified invalid token transition, excluding an arbitrarily long rejected continuation. A verified repair is a replacement supported by explicit protocol, execution, or task-level checks. The preferred and rejected action must share exactly the same conditioning history and tool schema; counterfactual execution also requires equivalent environment state. A later successful retry is not automatically a valid pair because its history contains additional observations.

Datakit is [Marin's data preparation and chat-rendering library](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit); DPO means direct preference optimization. Linked historical reports contain internal provenance paths and withheld-input references; they support public aggregate inspection, not complete independent replay.

Successful calls from otherwise unsuccessful trials are eligible positive examples. Record their evidence level: parser/schema validity, execution success, or task-verifier success. Do not equate these levels or put future tool results into the model's conditioning history.

Done when:

- Audit the existing training-complement corpus and publish eligible counts by harness, task, failure class, and evidence level. Report losses from missing exact histories or unreplayable state; do not presume a large usable yield.
- Implement deterministic extraction for unambiguous repairs and controlled corruptions of verified valid actions. Treat retry mining as a candidate source requiring prefix/state checks. Preserve originals, task/trajectory IDs, hashes, policy/harness versions, repair rules, and verification receipts.
- Emit standard preference artifacts with exact token histories and explicit supervised spans. Bound negative-action length, cap contributions per trajectory/task, deduplicate, and exclude holdout tasks and previously trained task identities as required by the experiment. Validate masks through the production renderer.
- Add behavior-focused tests for identical-prefix enforcement, task leakage, synthetic corruption validity, token-boundary preservation, and mask placement. Distinguish observed negatives from synthetic ones.
- Execute small controlled native DPO runs comparing the extracted local pairs with filtered whole-trace pairs and positive-only masked SFT. Explicitly configure beta, learning rate, sequence/token normalization, masks, batch composition, and reference initialization; vary one factor at a time where possible.
- Demonstrate actual updates and evaluate targeted validity/execution, task success, and cross-harness effects. Publish negative results and a reusable recipe even if DPO does not outperform the simpler control.
- Keep source datasets private unless independently cleared for redistribution; release tooling and aggregate evidence without proprietary harness scaffolding.

[Public collapse analysis](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/dpo-collapse-investigation-20261011.md) documents the rejected-loop imbalance motivating bounded examples. It does not prove that this change will repair the model. [Campaign closeout #10040](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040); related work: [localized online feedback #10043](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043) and [online multi-harness integration #10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041).

topics.title: Preserve BFCL recovery and shared-engine agent support
topics.body:
Preserve the BFCL recovery campaign's collection, preference curation, DPO, checkpoint export, and Daytona operations support. Retain task-split and trace provenance checks, assistant-only masks, and explicit treatment of malformed or repeated tool calls in preference data. Preserve explicit sharding in Snowball token reshapes and support CPU exports with a selected weight dtype and revision-pinned tokenizer.

Allow installed agents to request model turns through the shared RolloutEngine while it owns task machines, isolated grading, and exact-token training records. Support exact token-prefix replay and build versioned protocol diagnostics from BFCL tasks reserved and excluded from training before failure selection. The diagnostic checks tool-call syntax separately from task success.

Add BFCL training subsets checked against pinned task-content hashes and disjoint validation IDs. Pin task container images by digest and run grading in a separate machine that holds private grading files. Add a configurable final-token preference optimization (FTPO) recipe with the Pi agent, Daytona containers, BFCL-Parity task validation, and protocol diagnostic validation. Pin merged https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/980 at 37ec019b756cfd988ca8abd042cf25f24934224b. Its tree matches tested commit cb98adde74f1ee1c607e18e77d08483f3ae37ec0 and adds the repaired grading dependencies to the preceding PR #979 runtime. The training-token selector handles repeated `<tool_call>` openers separated by whitespace, including a first opener in the frozen assistant prompt. It also initializes missing optimizer state before a zero-update checkpoint save. Smoke `.13`, on the preceding runtime, saved a native checkpoint after one optimizer update; the zero-update case remains unverified in a live run.

Build training replays from task IDs assigned to training in the diagnostic's fixed split manifest. Check archive, tokenizer, and partition hashes; retain exact token prefixes and source-record identities; select the smallest prefix SHA-256 per task. Exclusions must specify a source-record ID and its exact conversion error. Collect all other conversion errors before rejecting the build. Input version `2026.10.11.4` contains 581 training prefixes from distinct tasks, 123 BFCL-Parity cases, and 156 diagnostic cases. Both validation sets are unchanged from version `2026.10.11.3`. Training and diagnostic prefix continuations do not execute tools. BFCL-Parity runs the Pi agent and its tools in Daytona containers.

Disable transitive uv source overrides in the isolated SkyRL launcher. A live smoke failed before GPU submission when a Git workspace supplied a development dependency below SkyRL's required version. The launch-composition tests now exercise the production bootstrap.

Reject explicitly unequal Megatron forward and training microbatches before submission. The next smoke allocated 192 GPUs before the runtime validator found this mismatch. The campaign now derives its forward microbatch from its training role plan. All 30 launcher tests and prepare-mode validation pass. Neither failed smoke reached model inference or training.

Scripted Daytona probes matched original grading in nine oracle/wrong/missing comparisons across three images in each of the training and evaluation accounts. The campaign evidence and remaining validation limits are recorded in #10040. Includes the Daytona runbook from #9858.

Set Pi's required `thinking_format` to `chat-template` for the hosted inference endpoint. Real Pi construction and prepare-mode validation pass. A live smoke exposed double-wrapped function definitions at the installed-agent boundary. The SkyRL pin converts these tools to the session's flat schema; its adapter-to-model-client regression and 2,504 CPU tests pass, with nine skipped.

A live Pi smoke generated model responses but failed BFCL grading because Pi supplies user content as text blocks. Normalize those blocks before constructing typed grading evidence. Preserve non-object JSON tool arguments as transcript evidence so file-based graders can run after rejected calls. Execution and final-action submissions still require argument objects; invalid JSON still fails at ingestion. A saved failing BFCL transcript now converts without changing its decoded arguments. Local tests cover correct and incorrect output files after a rejected call.

The grading repair passed 103 rollout tests and 497 TaskCompendium tests. One TaskCompendium failure depends on case-sensitive filenames and reproduces on unchanged main on this Mac. The affected workspace lane recorded 4,077 passes and four task-curation failures that also reproduce on main; the Haliax lane passed 387 tests. A review follow-up reuses Verifyit's duplicate-key decoder hook; 116 rollout and protocol tests pass. Adding that direct dependency to the lockfile selects the broad root suite. That run recorded 2,717 passes, the four task-curation failures, and one missing-bubblewrap collection error also reproduced on main. Lint and type checks pass. Run `2026.10.12.3` completed grading and retained scored and unscored validation records.

Request HF-format exports at checkpoint intervals and training end in the FTPO recipe. Smoke `.13` completed an optimizer update and saved a native checkpoint, but its coordinator failed during terminal export because the explicit callback list omitted export requests. A direct callback check now verifies checkpoint and export requests at terminal step 1, before the regular two-step interval is due. Run `2026.10.12.3` completed training and HF-format export, including verification of all 39 export shards and metadata consistency.

Expose learning rate and FTPO reference-regularization coefficient as required experiment inputs. Run `2026.10.12.3` completed four optimizer updates and reduced repeated tool-call openers from 69 to 3 among 156 diagnostic cases. Compared with the Recovery initializer, its matched policy evaluations improved MATH-500, HumanEval+, and BFCL-Parity, while IFBench strict-prompt accuracy declined from 73/300 to 68/300. Capability preservation remains unproven. Candidate `2026.10.12.4` changes only `lambda_mse` from 0.4 to 0.8. It passed prepare-mode validation but has not run.

The Daytona operations runbook now lives in #10110; the branch no longer carries it.

Part of #10040, #10041, and #10043.

topics.title: [canary-datakit-smoke] Store starves at one worker and times out
topics.body:
The tier-1 Datakit smoke ferry exceeded the 7,100-second Actions wait while `datakit/store` was still processing. The store requested 106 map workers; Iris ran one and left 105 pending. The root job had no task failures and was still running at 15:25 UTC.

Reproduce:
1. Run `.github/workflows/marin-canary-datakit-tier1.yaml` with the current `TIER1_SCALE` in `experiments/ferries/datakit_ferry.py`.
2. During `datakit/store`, inspect the clustered-store worker job under the ferry job. This run showed `pending=105 running=1`; `iris_monitor.py wait --timeout 7100` then raised `TimeoutError`.

Expected: the store gets enough workers to finish the ferry within the CI wait budget, or the run reports a placement failure before that deadline.

The coordinator reported `87/106 complete, 1 in-flight, 18 queued, 1/1 workers alive, 0 dead` at 15:18:57 UTC, when Actions timed out. The only running store worker was on a `v5e` TPU VM in `us-west4`; its request was 4 CPU, 32 GiB RAM, and 64 GiB disk. The configured CPU fallback has 16 GB RAM, so it cannot host this worker shape. The uploaded controller log shows the `us-west4` v5e pool scaling at 15:18 UTC. The specific placement verdict for the other 105 workers was unavailable; Iris showed no task events for a pending worker.

## Canary run context

- Lane: `datakit-smoke`; date: 2026-10-11 UTC
- Iris job: `/runner/iris-run-job-20261011-132010`
- [Actions run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/38142720107) and [uploaded diagnostics](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/38142720107/artifacts/11705653562)
- [W&B run URL](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/datakit-smoke-38142720107-1) (`datakit-smoke-38142720107-1`)

<details>
<summary>Exact checks</summary>

```text
15:18:57 Actions: TimeoutError after 7100.0s waiting for /runner/iris-run-job-20261011-132010
15:18:57 Finelog log: [stage0-Map] 87/106 complete, 1 in-flight, 18 queued, 1/1 workers alive, 0 dead
15:23:24 Iris worker job: Tasks 0/106 completed; pending=105, running=1
15:25:17 Iris root job: running, failures=0, preemptions=0
```

Finelog query: `marin` deployment, `log` namespace, exact coordinator attempt key, `epoch_ms` from 2026-10-11 15:18:30 to 15:19:05 UTC. The queried rows were present in the hub; recent forwarding can lag. The `zephyr.execution` record confirms 106 input shards. This is an infra/scheduling timeout, with the exact pending placement cause still unconfirmed.
</details>

topics.title: [grafana] Alert on failed hero attempts during retry initialization
topics.body:
An unexpected failure of a hero training attempt can be followed by an Iris retry without a critical Grafana alert during the interruption. `TrainingProgressStalled` resets its clock for the new execution and allows 45 minutes for initialization. `TrainingTelemetryGone` stops firing when the retry publishes `phase=initializing`. The warning-only `task_retried` check requires fresh training telemetry and an event from the last 15 minutes, so it can miss a retry that takes longer to initialize.

A [September 30 checkpoint failure](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/570) resumed training about 27 minutes after the last completed step. Neither critical rule fired during that gap. The checkpoint failure's initiating cause remains unconfirmed.

Done when: an unexpected failed attempt or retry of an enrolled hero run produces a critical alert during the interruption, including while its replacement initializes. Cover retry, recovery, and duplicate-notification behavior in tests.

topics.title: [iac] Allow the conversation worker to access its Marina applet
topics.body:
Allow the Iris conversation driver to reach its private Marina applet through `roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor` on the `marina` Cloud Run service in `us-central1`. Restrict the grant to `applets.marina.oa.dev` and the `/a/25f504c6-c6fb-4e14-8401-07dd8e6fbfba/` path.

The lab driver stopped advancing when its submitting laptop suspended. topics.title: [marina] Add job-scoped worker access to private applets
topics.body:
Background Iris jobs need to read and save data in private Marina applets without a developer's machine or login credentials. The conversation lab currently needs an IAP grant containing its exact applet UUID ([temporary grant PR #10050](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10050)). Repeating this for each applet makes application permissions depend on infrastructure changes.

Marina currently maps every IAP-authenticated caller to `admin` in [auth.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e449d03e35/infra/marina/src/marina/auth.py). Broadening the shared worker service account's IAP grant alone would admit workers to routes they should not access. A shared service-account identity also cannot distinguish individual Iris jobs.

Add reusable worker authentication and owner-managed delegation inside Marina. Infrastructure should admit Iris worker service-account identities through a stable policy. Marina should check access to each applet, and the applet should enforce permissions on its own resources, such as a conversation run. Use [Rigging’s request authentication and token verification](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging); credentials for this access must be scoped to Marina rather than accepting Iris control-plane tokens.

Done when:

- An applet owner can authorize a specific Iris job to read results, save traces, or claim queued work without another infrastructure PR. Grants identify the applet and permitted operations; the original user remains the owner.
- Marina verifies the individual job identity. Another job using the same machine service account cannot reuse that job's permissions.
- Worker access does not permit publishing applets, changing grants, controlling unrelated runs, or accessing unassigned private applets. Resource-specific permissions are enforced by the applet backend.
- Workers use renewable credentials without copied human refresh tokens. An owner can revoke delegation, and later requests fail even while the underlying machine credentials remain valid.
- Authorization tests cover allowed operations, another job on the same service account, another applet, revoked grants, and attempts to use worker access on management routes.
- The existing conversation lab migrates to this mechanism before its UUID-specific IAP exception is removed. Document worker setup and the authorization boundary for applet authors.

[The recovery incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/701) records why the lab driver moved from a laptop to an always-on Iris job.

topics.title: [datakit] Release the shared Zephyr pool after its last stage
topics.body:
Release the shared Zephyr pool when its last stage succeeds, so idle shared workers stop holding hosts needed by dedicated pools. `run_reference_steps` runs normalization before starting the shared pool; a watcher thread calls `ZephyrContext.shutdown()` after every step in `DatakitSteps.shared_pool_steps` succeeds. All three ferries use this path through `run_reference_ferry`, as does `reference_pipeline.py --target all`. The shared pool uses `_IdleWorkerPolicy.RETAIN`, so it previously kept every acquired worker until the DAG ended: up to 512 workers (2 CPU / 16 GiB each) on v5e hosts, while the embed, quality, fuzzy-cluster, and store pools waited for hosts.

Reduce the tier-1 store worker from 4 CPU / 32 GiB RAM / 64 GiB disk to 2 CPU / 8 GiB RAM / 16 GiB disk. A store task with one normalized shard peaks below 2 GiB RAM and spills below 1 GiB. On 2026-10-12, the old shape received 1 of 106 workers; the new shape received 12 workers in 1 minute.

On the fixed code, tier 1 (`/rav/iris-run-job-20261012-153556`) succeeded in 56 minutes. Tier 3 (`/rav/iris-run-job-20261012-153605`) succeeded, and its shared pool stopped at 19:30 UTC after fuzzy dedup. Tier 3 took 5h47m, exceeding the 20,700-second CI wait. On a busy cluster, the shared pool received only 275 of its 512 workers, and tokenization took 2h37m, compared with 37 minutes on 2026-10-05.

The tier-3 fuzzy-cluster workers drop from 16 CPU / 128 GiB / 64 GiB disk to 8 CPU / 64 GiB / 32 GiB, with 64 instead of 32 workers, so the task count stays at 512. Only one of the larger workers fits on a v5e host. On 2026-10-13 the verify workers waited 3h46m for hosts, and the tier-3 ferry took 7h30m. At 16 tasks per worker, cluster text peaked at 66 GiB and verify at 26 GiB.

The three tiers passed in CI on this branch. Tier 1 took 56 minutes, and tier 2 took 1h51m. Tier 3 (`/runner/iris-run-job-20261013-165715`) took 2h25m, with 36 minutes for fuzzy verification. This is much less than the 20,700-second CI wait.

The tier concurrency groups now include `github.ref`, so a run started on a branch and the scheduled run on main do not cancel each other.

Fixes https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10047. Fixes https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10059.

topics.title: [zephyr] Cap native thread pools at the worker's and task's CPU share
topics.body:
Native thread pools (Polars, OpenMP for faiss/torch/numba/Arrow, OpenBLAS,
MKL, numba, rayon for HF tokenizers) size themselves from the node's core
count and read their cap once, at import or first pool use. An Iris task pod
on CoreWeave carries only a CPU request, so a 2-CPU Zephyr worker starts
pools sized for the whole node. The four InlineRunner stages (embed, quality
score, centroid sample, domain assign) run inside the worker actor process,
where polars/pyarrow/numpy are imported before any task runs, so nothing
inside a task can lower the cap. Today only SubprocessRunner children are
capped, and only for Polars.

`memory_budget.native_thread_env(cpu)` returns `POLARS_MAX_THREADS`,
`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS`,
`NUMBA_NUM_THREADS` and `RAYON_NUM_THREADS`, each `max(1, ceil(cpu))`. It is
applied at the two boundaries that are pre-import by construction:

- the Iris environment of the coordinator and worker actor-group jobs, via a
  new optional `environment` keyword on fray `create_actor_group` (forwarded
  by the Iris backend, ignored by `LocalClient`, whose actors are threads);
- the SubprocessRunner child env, which now carries the full map at task cpu
  instead of `POLARS_MAX_THREADS` alone. Arrow in shard children stays
  API-pinned to 1.

No process writes `os.environ`, and no threads or buffers are added, so
memory can only fall. `thread_cap_environment` passes `workspace=os.getcwd()`
only because `EnvironmentConfig` requires a workspace or an image;
`convert_environment` reads only `env_vars`. Narrowing the fray keyword to
`env_vars: dict[str, str]` would drop that placeholder at the cost of
diverging from `JobRequest.environment`; happy to switch if preferred.

## Measurements

Proxy kernels standing in for each stage, on a 16-CPU VM with no CPU quota:
8 fresh 2-CPU-shaped processes at once, 3 repeats, median, clean environment
vs `native_thread_env(2)`:

| kernel | wall p50 | CPU-s per repeat | max RSS | involuntary ctx switches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| assign (faiss) | 68.8 -> 11.8 s | 1082 -> 181 | flat | 10.7M -> 10k |
| embed (numba + OpenBLAS) | 21.7 -> 21.0 s | 303 -> 274 | -300 MB | -65% |
| reader (Arrow) | 7.7 -> 7.65 s | 73 -> 68 | -57 MB | -83% |
| shuffle (Polars) | 8.6 -> 7.9 s | 124 -> 110 | -840 MB | -94% |

The capped version lands within noise of pinning each process to 2 cores
with `taskset` on every kernel. Under a `CPUQuota=200%` cgroup (GCP
preemptible shape) assign and embed gain the same; shuffle is flat because
Polars already sizes from the quota. One process alone on an idle 16-core
box is slower (2 threads instead of 16), a shape no production worker has;
the same process under a 2-CPU quota is 63% (assign) and 57% (embed) faster.
Result hashes are identical in every arm.

A local datakit pipeline under SubprocessRunner (task cpu 1 and 2.5, main vs
branch) is byte-identical with worker mem_peak ratio 1.004 and 1.001.
Fresh-interpreter probes under `native_thread_env(2)` show every covered
library reporting 2 threads.

Not measured: the CoreWeave pod shape (CPU request only, no `limits.cpu` or
cpuset) is read from the Iris k8s backend
(`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py`), not observed on a
cluster, and the stage-level production gain is extrapolated from the
kernels.

Out of scope: quality score (XLA's CPU pool ignores all six variables and
needs sched affinity), tokenizer parallelism in shard children
(`TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=false` stays), the store worker's
partition-process Arrow pin, and `pa.io_thread_count`.

## Tests

- SubprocessRunner map returns `pl.thread_pool_size() == ceil(task cpu)` on
  a cpu=4 worker (1 -> 1, 2.5 -> 3).
- A fresh interpreter under `native_thread_env(1.5)` reports Polars and Arrow
  pools of 2.
- The fray Iris backend submits explicit env vars merged over device
  defaults.
- A `requires_cluster` test observes (2, 2) from an inline stage on a cpu=2
  Iris worker.

topics.title: [rl] Integrate sampled grading with curation and Atlas
topics.body:
FULL RL curation now samples the resulting TaskSpec parquet and stage evidence, prepares bounded packets with Zephyr, and obtains one structured GLM judgment per item. The default sample contains up to 100 retained tasks and 20 excluded diagnostics. SAMPLE campaigns opt in with `--assess`. The artifact graph connects curation, packet preparation and grading; a rubric or model change reuses curation outputs.

Executable controls and downstream grades have separate policies. A control sample passing at least 95% allows curation to skip unsampled controls. Otherwise it validates eligible tasks individually, retaining passes, rejecting failures and deferring unavailable controls. Checkpoints preserve completed trials on retries. Downstream grading labels a source Good when at least 80% of judgments are Good and Bad when more than 20% are Bad. If neither threshold is met, fewer than 80% conclusive judgments means Unknown; otherwise the label is Some issues. Completed curation that retains no tasks is Bad. Excluded diagnostics do not affect the source grade, and grading does not change task admission. Large tasks retain bounded summaries with explicit omissions.

The typed catalog owns source declarations, assessment keys, populations, judgments and archived evidence. Atlas reads Postgres through an explicit staged catalog load. SQL computes counts and grades; the browser handles filtering, sorting and CSV export. Unchanged snapshots skip loading. Inventory-only sources carry a skip reason. The separate reassessment path, manual verifier declarations and legacy review-publication code path are removed; historical manual reviews remain archived.

The completed campaign covers all 146 curation pipelines in an inventory of 206 sources. The selected catalog snapshot is `8c5d247ef6c2416fb3d14b2f159f74c4`: 63 Good, 40 Some issues, 43 Bad and 0 Unknown. Forty-one Bad sources retained no tasks; two exceeded the Bad judgment threshold. All retained samples have TaskSpecs and conclusive judgments.

| Sample cohort | Items | Good | Some issues | Bad | Unknown |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Retained | 10,430 | 8,513 | 1,458 | 459 | 0 |
| Excluded diagnostics | 1,677 | 235 | 150 | 977 | 315 |

The local AIME24/SVAMP rollout took 6.4 seconds for six SAMPLE judgments (five retained tasks and one excluded diagnostic) and 0.33 seconds on an unchanged repeat. The first aggregation left 72 sources Unknown; 41 became Bad under the zero-output rule and 31 were regraded after packet and control-validation fixes. A final campaign reused those 31 assessment graphs and published one catalog snapshot with the other 115 assessments retained. The regional archive audit checked all 12,107 packets in 125 seconds: 284.7 MB total and 50.8 KB at p95. Bulk GCS processing stayed in us-central2. [Campaign outputs](https://console.cloud.google.com/storage/browser/marin-us-central2/rl-data-curation-assessment/2026-10-12-campaign/campaigns) include `updated-grade-report.md` with every source's sample scores, control outcomes and inference measurements. Permanent catalog and evidence outputs are under `gs://marin-us-central2/rl-data-curation-assessment/2026-10-12-campaign/campaigns/`.

The live Atlas applet remains on its previous revision because Marina requires its current publisher to deploy the bundle and load this catalog.

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the build step DAG and its memo store
topics.body:
Add the author and build stages of Taskforge as `stage30_author` and `stage40_build`. An author writes async steps decorated with `@rl_env_build_step`, which takes a step's inputs from its parameters after the context, and a final step decorated with `@rl_env_build_sink`, which reads its inputs the same way and refuses any return annotation other than `TaskSpec`. `rl_env_build_program(*steps, sink=...)` orders the steps by Kahn's algorithm, breaking ties by declaration order and running the sink last. It refuses duplicate names, unknown inputs, cycles, a step taking the sink as an input, and a step whose output reaches neither another step nor the sink, since that output would never enter the task. A step receives an `RLEnvBuildContext` (item id, model, sampling policy) and then its inputs by name, where a parameter called `proposal` receives the caller's proposal, an opaque JSON value at this point in the stack. `static_author` hands back a hand-written program as an author. `run_program` returns the sink's `TaskSpec`, and `run_build` writes it to `draft/task.json` with an `ItemBuildProvenance` in `draft/provenance.json`, which lists every step's stored memo beside that build's hit or miss status for it. The status belongs to the build and stays out of the stored memo, which the store writes only on a miss.

Each step's output is memoized under a key of `SDK_VERSION`, the sha256 of the step's own source, the content digest of each declared input, and a model digest over the model id and the sampling policy. Because inputs enter the key by content, a step that reruns with an identical output leaves its consumers cached. A helper read from outside a step body is not in the key, so changing one needs a declared input or an `SDK_VERSION` bump. Item ids belong to the caller and are only checked for file safety.

The store is a hand-rolled memo of about 60 lines over rigging's `StoragePath` and `atomic_rename`, holding content-addressed JSON blobs and per-item memos under a local path or an object-store URL. joblib keys on function identity and clears a function's whole cache when its code changes, so it reuses nothing across program revisions, and Marin's `StepSpec` hashes no code and costs a status file and a distributed lock per step. Its `load` and `store` take a caller-built key, and `memoized` is the one call the runner and a driver use, so a driver can memoize a helper against the same store with a key it builds. `memoized(store, name, key, output_type, compute)` loads under such a key and on a miss awaits `compute` and stores the result, and `run_program` calls it for every step.

Stage packages are numbered by tens in pipeline order (proposal 10, triage 20, author 30, build 40), and `tests/test_imports.py` fails when a stage imports a higher-numbered one.

The design comes from draft #9993. Later PRs bring back the proposal package, the ledger, the author's programs written by the language model, the validate and review stages, and the stage coordinator.

topics.title: [grug] Add a separate QK multiplier for hero global layers
topics.body:
Add `GrugModelConfig.qk_mult_long_scale`, an extra Q multiplier on the hero's global layers (every `global_every`-th layer and the last: full causal, RoPE disabled). Global layers multiply Q by `qk_mult` and then by `qk_mult_long_scale`. Local sliding-window layers use `qk_mult` alone. The field, its 1.0 default, and the order of the two multiplies match `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/model.py` and the pinned vLLM GrugMoE backend, which reads the same config key. A scale of 1.0 adds no op, so the live hero and existing checkpoints trace unchanged. Otherwise the layer scan's traced `is_global` flag selects the scale with `jnp.where`, which keeps one scan body for all layers and covers both RoPE paths.

Q and K are RMS-normalized, so the Q multiplier sets the softmax temperature. Moving the hero from 4K to 16K context leaves the local layers' 2048-token window unchanged, so the YaRN-style mscale, 1.3 × (0.1·ln(s) + 1), applies only to the global layers. Trial arms can raise the global scale and hold the local layers at 1.3: a long scale of 1.1386 gives 1.48, and 1.2964 gives 1.68.

The HF config export writes `qk_mult_long_scale`. A config without the key loads with 1.0. `launch_diagnostics.py` takes `--qk-mult-long-scale`. `launch_scaling_ladder.py` and `trigger_hero.sh` are unchanged because #9689 also changes them; the production flag will follow after it lands.

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the stage coordinator over the build DAG
topics.body:
Add `stage_coordinator`, which runs an item through triage, author, build, validate and review with the stage functions a caller passes in `StageFunctions`. Each stage returns an event with an exit, and a transition table gives the next stage. The item's state is a fold over its events (`derive_state`). `ItemBudget` bounds build revisions and validation retries, and the coordinator spends them when it records `AUTHOR_FAILED`, `BUILD_FAILED` or `DECIDED`. A build error from the program's own code, `BuildFailure` or any other exception, costs a revision. `BuildInfrastructureFailure` (the build host failed: a sandbox did not start, an image did not pull, a pod died), `ModelUnavailable` and `OSError` (a storage fault, a missing blob or memo) are failures the author cannot fix. Those fail the item in place at the build stage, and the next `run_item` builds the same program again with its revisions unspent. When the author raises `StructuredOutputError` because its structured reply stayed invalid after the repair turn, as when the output limit cut it, the coordinator records `AUTHOR_FAILED`, spends a revision from the same budget, and asks the author again with `Revision(AUTHOR_FAILURE, ...)`.

The `OPENED` event records the digests of the proposal and the budget, and the coordinator's model digest, the model part of every step key. A relaunch with any of them changed raises `ValueError`, so every build of an item runs under one model. The author returns an `AuthoredProgram`, the program with the Python source it came from. The coordinator writes the source to `rounds/<n>/authored/<k>/program.py`, beside the manifest `program.json`, with `k` the item's build failures so far. The build stage loads the program from that file with `StageFunctions.load_program`, so a sampling model author is called once per revision. Each author call gets its own directory, so a process killed after re-authoring leaves the program of the saved `AUTHORED` event in place for the relaunch. `stage30_author/loader.py` is the plain loader; the author PR replaces it with a restricted one (allowed imports, safe builtins). A program defined in Python, as `static_author` returns, has no source, and for it the build stage asks the author again. In both cases a build whose program digest differs from the `AUTHORED` event raises.

Events stay in an `ItemEventLog` (in memory here) while the item runs. When the item reaches a terminal, `run_item` saves the log through an `ItemEventStore`. `JsonEventStore` writes `items/<item_id>/events.json` after every other file of the item, and the next `run_item` with an empty log restores the log from it. An accepted or rejected item then returns without running a stage or writing a byte. When the store lacks the final log, as after a failed save retried with the same in-memory log, `run_item` saves it before returning. An abandoned item re-enters validation with its retries reset, and a failed item resumes at the stage that raised, with the step store under `<root>/store` serving the build steps already run. A process killed mid-item restarts from the last saved terminal, or from triage. The ledger PR adds a file-backed log saving each event on append.

The triage verdict and the review `Decision` types come along as the vocabulary the machine records; `Retry.cause` and `Modify.findings` are strings until validate returns. Validate and review are caller functions: the coordinator writes the validate summary to `validation.json` and passes review the JSON read back from it. `stage_coordinator` sits above the numbered stages and may import every one of them, and nothing imports it. The capability experiment runs a catalog entry through the coordinator with its example program as a sink-only build, to an accepted task.

The design is cut from draft #9993, and the base is #10081.

topics.title: [task-curation] Add Dockerfile toolchain fragments and a Lean grader image
topics.body:
An `Environment` can name a checked-in, self-contained Dockerfile fragment that installs a toolchain the package lock cannot provide. A fragment forces placement in a built image, its bytes enter the environment identity, the build refuses an untracked fragment, and the generated Dockerfile runs its lines after the apt step and before the lock sync so toolchain layers stay cached across lock changes. A fragment may use only `ARG`, `ENV` and `RUN`; the declaration refuses `FROM`, `USER`, `WORKDIR`, `SHELL`, `COPY`, `ADD`, `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD`, which would replace the base, break the generated package steps or change the grader container. The existing build CLI pushes the image to the public iris-task package and records its digest, so pinning follows from the identity.

The environment artifact record now carries the identity, the built image digest, and the lock digest and `data` the worker runtime reads back from the record beside the lock. The copies of `apt`, the Python version, the base image, the fragment digest and the pushed tag are gone; the identity already hashes them and nothing read them.

`LEAN_GRADER_PACKAGES` uses the fragment to add elan, Lean leanprover/lean4 v4.12.0 and Mathlib v4.12.0 (commit 809c3fb3) with prebuilt oleans at `/lean4/my_project`, the layout the NeMo Skills sandbox uses, so the vendored Lean feedback parser finds diagnostics at the path it expects. `LocalLeanSandbox` compiles a proof with `lake env lean` in that project and answers with the NeMo Skills server's `lean4` response fields. The Nemotron Ultra Lean grader can then run inside the network-denied grader sandbox instead of calling an in-cluster sandbox service. This PR adds the image and the sandbox class only; the Lean converter and controls land in #10077.

The image built locally in 109 s for the Lean and Mathlib layer (2.39 GB; 3.8 GB total). With networking disabled and as uid 65534, a Mathlib `simp` proof completes in 4 s warm and 38 s cold, a bad tactic fails with the diagnostic at the project path, and a `sorry` proof completes with the warning the status parser maps to `has_sorry`. The cold time exceeds the vendored scorer's default 30 s timeout, so the converter needs a larger timeout. The Lean and Mathlib pins match every NeMo Skills sandbox build since October 2024; the private sandbox image MarinSkyRL pins by digest does not record its revision, so the pin is not confirmed against that exact image. No artifact for the environment has been built or pushed yet.

topics.title: [agents] Add the pr-review-doc skill
topics.body:
pr-review-doc makes a "Review Doc" for a PR: a Google Doc of at most 3 pages
in the shared pr_reviews Drive folder. The doc tells why the PR exists, how the
code works before the PR, how the PR changes it, and its limits, with a
component diagram and code snippets. If the doc cannot explain the PR in 3
pages, it recommends a split.

A background design and simplicity review fills the Review section of the doc
when it completes. Then the skill answers comments in the doc and corrects the
doc when a comment finds an error. When the user asks, it posts the review as
inline PR comments, after the user approves the exact draft.

topics.title: [taskforge] State field bounds in the structured-output instruction
topics.body:
`schema_instruction` now states each field's JSON-schema constraints in words after its type, covering length and item-count bounds, numeric bounds, enum and const values, and patterns, as in `notes (string, at most 1000 characters, required)`, with item bounds on lists prefixed by `each`.
The server's grammar already enforced these bounds without the instruction stating them, so on a live run with a `max_length=1000` field the model drafted 1,100 to 1,400 characters and 16 of 19 replies stopped at exactly 1,000 where the grammar closed the string mid-word.
After the cut, the model wrote a stub into the next field or emitted whitespace between JSON members until max_tokens, and one reply held 131,072 tokens of whitespace.
The instruction also renders models nested at any depth, indenting each level under its field with the nested model's docstring as the first line, and writes a model that recurs inside itself as one line such as `Section (same fields as above)`, so a constraint stated on a field of a model inside a list now reaches the prompt without the caller repeating it.

topics.title: [haliax] Run the tile-map ragged_dot kernels on NVIDIA GPUs
topics.body:
Hopper (sm_90) and data-center Blackwell (sm_100 and sm_103) GPUs now run the Pallas-Triton grouped GEMM behind `ragged_dot` with the tile-map kernels from #10009, which AMD Instinct GPUs already use. Until now they ran the group-grid kernels, which launch a full row grid for every expert. Other NVIDIA GPUs, such as A100 and consumer Blackwell (sm_120), keep the group-grid kernels: the tuned configs need about 192 KiB of shared memory per block in bf16, more than those GPUs allow. Block configs were swept on H100 and GB200 at the June (G=32, K and N of 1280-2560) and Mixtral-like (G=8, 4096x14336) expert shapes. On H100, drhs (the weight gradient) uses 128x128x32 blocks below 2048 rows per expert; with the 128x256x64 blocks it uses above that, it was 4-8% slower than group-grid at 512 rows per expert.

Per call in bf16, against group-grid, at M from 16384 to 196608 rows with balanced and Zipf-skewed routing:

| GPU | Tile-map faster | Speedup |
|---|---|---|
| GB200 | 54 of 54 cases | 1.03-2.47x |
| H100 | 49 of 54 cases | 1.04-2.50x |

The other 5 H100 cases are drhs at 512 and 1024 rows per expert, at 0.98-1.00x.

On one 8xH100 node, an 8-layer June model (batch 64, 8-way expert parallelism, full recompute) took 0.817 s per step with tile-map and 0.848-0.849 s in three group-grid runs, a 3.9% throughput gain, with the same loss after 20 steps.

`lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py --kernel-families group_grid tile_map` reproduces the balanced per-call timings.

topics.title: [grug] Hero vibe-check samples pre-switch checkpoints with the current model config
topics.body:
The hero completions sampler stamps every discovered checkpoint with the current `HERO_MODEL_CONFIG`, so after the 16K context switch (#9615) a rebuilt or re-released sample store would sample checkpoints from before step 257553 with `qk_mult` 1.48 instead of the 1.3 they trained with. Nothing flags the mismatch, because `model` is excluded from `sample_id`.

Requests already in the store are safe: `SampleStore.save_request` writes a request only once, and the stored requests for steps 246000, 252000, and 257553 record `qk_mult` 1.3 and `max_seq_len` 4096. The risk appears only when `spec.release` is bumped (the documented backfill knob) or the store root changes.

`sampling_model()` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ops/vibe_check/config.py` should choose the model per checkpoint. `hero_checkpoint_paths` already reads each ancestor run's W&B config and could carry its `model` along; alternatively the context history could record `qk_mult` per phase.

Found in the independent review of the 16K deploy PR.

topics.title: [grug] Switch the hero to 16K context with qk_mult 1.48
topics.body:
Switch the hero from 4K to 16K context with `qk_mult` 1.48 on all layers. The new run `hero-ctx16k-step257k` forks `hero-mfu30-step231k` at its permanent `step-257553`, where the parent stopped on 2026-10-13. Tokens per rack per update, the 390251-step schedule, and the optimizer stay the same, so the batch drops from 11264 to 2816 sequences on 11 racks.

`HERO_MODEL` gets `max_seq_len=16384` and `qk_mult=1.48`. `HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES` records the 4K phase ending at step 257553, and `HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL` is 1.7792877262736668e24, the parent's `throughput/total_gflops` × 1e9 at W&B `_step` 257552 (`global_step` 257552). `trigger_hero.sh` hands off from `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-mfu30-step231k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-257553` (permanent, `metadata.json` step 257553) and forks W&B at `hero-mfu30-step231k?_step=257552`; `current_run.py` names the child.

`build_ladder_run` now uses the checked-in history for d6144 by itself instead of relying on `main()`, and it refuses an explicit `num_steps` while a history is in effect, because the prior phases' data stages are rebuilt from the schedule length. The diagnostics launcher and restore benchmark take their default batch from the hero's tokens per rack at the model's context length (256 sequences per rack at 16K); the old fixed 1024-sequence default would have put four times the hero's load on a rack. `HERO_EP_BATCH_SIZE` is replaced by `HERO_TOKENS_PER_RACK` and `hero_rack_batch_size` in `hero_recipe.py`.

In 100-step arms at 16K from permanent `step-252000` on the 11 hero racks (#9615), the dropless eval loss after step 252100 was 1.81349 at `qk_mult` 1.3, 1.81156 at 1.48, 1.81200 at 1.58, and 1.81282 for 1.68 on the global layers only. The differences are within eval noise, so we keep the YaRN-style value 1.3 × (0.1·ln 4 + 1). Those arms also ran the 16K dropless eval on 11 racks at 123.4 GiB peak memory, about 30.6% MFU, and a drop fraction falling to about 1.2e-3.

A dry build of the exact `trigger_hero.sh` launch gives 16K, `qk_mult` 1.48/1.0, capacity 1.15, batch 2816, eval at the training length every 3000 steps, `FlopsBaseline(257553, 1.7792877e24)`, and a rebuilt 4K phase with stages [0, 108000, 312192] at batch 11264. The optimizer config is identical to main's 4K build and to the parent's logged config, and the rebuilt phase's mixture, shuffle, and seed match what the parent trained with. An independent review found no blockers; its findings are fixed here except the vibe-check sampler, filed as #10100.

- Run `trigger_hero.sh fork-wandb` right after merge. Until the child exists and logs its config, the hourly completions workflow fails at `hero_checkpoint_paths`.
- The parent stopped at the handoff, so there is no same-batch control window. The agreed gates: the first logged step is 257553 and cross-entropy stays below 1.25 over the first 10 steps; cross-entropy in 1.09–1.15; MFU at least 29% after warmup; drop fraction below 2e-3 by step 257633–257652; peak memory 123–124 GiB; no retries, watchdogs, or runtime errors; the first 16K eval at step 258000 completes.
- Rollback relaunches `f2bc69bf6c` under `hero-mfu30-step231k`, which resumes `step-257553`.
- Eval packs at 16K from the child onward, so the `eval_dropless/*` series step down at the switch, and `eval_regressed` may fire once.
- Comparison report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Hero-16K-cutover:-hero-ctx16k-step257k-trial--VmlldzoxODEwNzE3Mg==

@ClassicLarry for review.

topics.title: [taskcompendium] Start grading in the grader workspace
topics.body:
The grading machine now starts in the grader's workspace unless its environment specifies a `working_directory`. This restores the behavior before #10021 when the environment names no directory and preserves an explicit directory when it does.

Since #10021, every script-graded task has failed while creating its grading machine on Iris. `_grade_staged` previously passed `workdir=grading.workspace`; the move to `prepare_machine_spec` dropped that argument. When the grader environment names no directory, `prepare_machine_spec` retains the spec's workdir, which is empty for an image machine because `rolloutengine._machine_spec` leaves it empty. Docker interprets an empty workdir as the image's `WORKDIR`, so laptop grading continued to work. Iris instead runs `mkdir -p ""` and fails:

```
RuntimeError: Failed to create Iris workdir : mkdir: cannot create directory ''
```

The Taskforge ladder dry run on cw-rno2a hit this failure in every grader sandbox. Solver and control machines were unaffected because `draft.requirements` names `/workspace`.

A test checks the spec passed to the factory with and without an explicit `working_directory`; the grader-workspace case fails on main. The ShellSim-backed taskcompendium suite passed locally. The bubblewrap-backed tests require Linux, and CI runs the full suite.

topics.title: [task-curation] Declare grader requirements, files and env
topics.body:
An `Environment` declares what a grader environment wants, and the build resolves it:

- `requirements`: exact `name==version` pins or `name @ https://...` URLs naming a commit. The build compiles them with `uv pip compile --generate-hashes --exclude-newer <date>` and stores the lock in the artifact; the cutoff date is a constant in the build module and part of the identity, so every build of an identity resolves the same transitive packages. `grader.in` and `grader.lock` are deleted; the pins live in `datasets/environments.py` as per-scorer tuples, and the four previously unpinned entries take the versions the lock had resolved.
- `files`: absolute guest paths, each receiving a member of an https archive pinned by URL and SHA-256. The build downloads, verifies and extracts the member into the build context. A built image gets `COPY files/ /`; the artifact stores `files.tar` and `environment.json` (paths, archive digest, env) for the worker. A path under a host system directory, which bubblewrap binds read-only, or inside another placed path is rejected at declaration.
- `env`: variables for the grader in both placements, rendered as `ENV` lines in the image and set on the worker sandbox.
- `apt`, `image` and `dockerfile` are unchanged.

The NLTK-only `data` slot is gone. `GRADER_PACKAGES` places the English `punkt_tab` tokenizer from a pinned `nltk_data` archive at `/srv/nltk_data/tokenizers/punkt_tab/english` with `NLTK_DATA=/srv/nltk_data`. `wordnet` had no consumer and is dropped. The Punkt models carry no license in `nltk_data`, so the tables are fetched at build time rather than checked in.

The worker runtime downloads the lock and hashes it itself instead of reading a digest from the artifact record, and reads `environment.json` and `files.tar` beside the lock when present; the lock and archive digests both enter the cached environment's identity. `taskcompendium.runtime.local` loses `LockEnvironment`, the `.artifact.json` reader and the NLTK downloader. The artifact record keeps only the identity and the built image digest.

shellbox's `HostImage` gains `mounts`, host files or directories shown read-only at another guest path with a plain `--ro-bind`. The local backend treats its read-only directories as mounts at their own paths and refuses a guest path inside a system directory, inside another mount, or as the workdir; uploads to a mounted path are rejected. QUICK mode records the lock URL the environment's artifact would have under the active artifact prefix.

Placement does not change: the base grader and compiler environments run in bubblewrap on the Zephyr worker, and Lean runs in its built image. The first `python -m experiments.post_training.task_curation.images --all` build verifies the `punkt_tab` archive digest against the live download.

topics.title: [grug] Run the ring EP MoE test's collectives synchronously on AMD GPUs
topics.body:
On AMD GPUs, the forward and gradient jits in `test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available` now pass the compiler option `xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES`, so each device runs one collective at a time. The test checks for the ROCm backend, so this covers both MI300X and MI350X. CUDA and TPU keep XLA's default collective schedule, as in training. Only the test changes.

On 8x MI300X without the fix, the ring-backend cases `[all_valid-ring]` and `[padded-ring]` hung until the pytest timeout in 10 of 52 runs, where each run is one fresh pytest process for one case. The hangs happened on both cluster nodes, and on main from both before and after #9860 added `ring_gather_combine`. The ring forward launches its psum-scatter over the expert axis (a 2-device RCCL communicator) asynchronously on a second stream. The drop-count psum over all 8 devices does not depend on it, so it runs on the compute stream while the psum-scatter is in flight. In the backward, the weight-gradient psum over the data axis (4 devices) overlaps the same psum-scatter. Because the two collectives run on different streams, nothing fixes which one each GPU runs first, so the order can differ between ranks and between runs. In hung runs, rocgdb showed one RCCL kernel running on every GPU and work pending on a second hardware queue, consistent with each rank waiting for peers that are in the other collective. NCCL documents that operations on different communicators can deadlock when ranks issue them in different orders ([Using multiple NCCL communicators concurrently](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/usage/communicators.html#using-multiple-nccl-communicators-concurrently)).

On MI300X with the fix, the two cases passed 24 of 24 runs (12 per case), and RCCL logs showed each device launching all of its collectives on one stream. The same flag set through `XLA_FLAGS` on unmodified main also passed 24 of 24.

On 8x MI350X, unmodified main hung in 2 of 24 runs (12 per case), back to back on one node, after every GPU had launched the same overlapping collectives. In both hangs only one GPU still had an RCCL kernel running and queued work, while the other seven had drained their queues. On MI300X every GPU was still waiting, so the MI350X hang may have a different cause that synchronous collectives do not prevent. With the fix, MI350X passed 8 of 8 runs. At main's hang rate, 8 runs in a row pass about half the time without the fix, so this does not yet show that the fix holds on MI350X.

On 8x H100, unmodified main passed all 48 runs (24 per case), although NCCL logs showed the same overlap. NCCL's warning applies to NVIDIA GPUs too, so CUDA may still hang at a lower rate; 48 clean runs put that rate below about 6% per run at 95% confidence. CUDA keeps XLA's default schedule so the test compiles as training does there.

Training still runs the ring EP backends with async collectives, so AMD training could hit the same overlap. We have not seen this hang in training or measured what synchronous collectives would cost there. Only one ragged all-to-all EP configuration in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py` forces synchronous collectives, after overlapping collectives there hung or gave run-to-run different gradients on GB200.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [grug] Add the quality-classifier fast track
topics.body:
* add the quality-classifier fast track: for each rung budget `B`, score the first `10·B` tokens of a fixed raw pool, keep the top whole documents until they fill `B`, and train the fast-track ladder on them
  * this PR holds only the quality track from #9371 [^1]
* `corpus_sample_cli` builds a `RawCorpusPool` from the registered DataKit sources in proportion to corpus size with `corpus-id-interval-v1`: one seeded cyclic interval in the 128-bit document-ID space for each source. it skips a row group only when its ID statistics show no overlap
  * `--label-exclusion-manifest` is required, so the pool contains no labelled duplicate group
  * one map task reads 64 normalized shards, with 128 workers. a 291-source pool has 149,717 shards. one task for each shard with 8 workers did about 100 shards a minute, and each reducer had to merge one scatter output per shard. the 10.7B-token pool now takes 25 min
* `quality_labels_cli` freezes the GLM-5.2 labels and fits a ridge head on cached Harrier features (target `(quality - 1) / 4`, 80/10/10 split by duplicate group)
* `quality_cli --stage features|score|select|train` scores the pool one time at the largest rung, then selects and trains each rung from the same `ScoredPool`
  * `--selection-method candidate|incumbent|random`. `random` ranks the same `10·B` prefix by a seeded hash and is the matched control
  * a custom scorer is a `module:factory` that returns a `DocumentQualityScorer`, with a JSON `--classifier-identity`
  * the selected documents keep the raw-pool order, so scores do not change the training order
  * the feature stage joins the complete Harrier pins (`hero_data.pinned_map("harrier")`, not the `hero_data.harrier` `StepSpec`) and converts only the selected rows of each row group [^2]
* add `fast-track-long-string-v1` for raw-corpus tokenization: split at the first whitespace at or after 10,000 characters, and reject a document above 64 MiB with its source and ID
  * bound native tokenizer batches by bytes. a local 32 MiB probe kept all 19,532,169 token IDs, and peak RSS went from 4.60 GiB to 2.85 GiB
* `launch.py` resolves the rung budget in `resolve_h100_ladder_budget` and takes a `TrainingSource`, so the quality track uses the same training wiring as `fast-track`
  * add `--seed` and `--data-seed`. `--submit` forwards `WANDB_MODE` and accepts `WANDB_MODE=disabled` without `WANDB_API_KEY`
  * the quality CLIs default to MoE and `d512`, and derive `--data-seed` from `--seed`
* run fixes
  * iris: repair missing CUDA toolchain files. put the child job and attempt in JAX coordinator names, because sibling training jobs connected to the coordinator of a different job
  * fray: pass actor concurrency to Iris RPC servers, because the 32-thread default let long waits block worker heartbeats. the inference broker sets its concurrency explicitly
  * datakit CPU drivers install the `cpu` group with `datakit`, so that they do not resolve the CUDA Torch wheel
  * artifact loading keeps absolute bucket paths, grug dispatch forwards `WANDB_MODE`, and levanter keeps eval metrics between detail intervals
* validation on `cw-us-east-02a`: one 10,695,475,362-token pool from the 291 sources other than `stack-v3`, scored one time at d768, dense models, final eval loss from the training logs [^3]

  | run | selection | Paloma macro | Uncheatable macro |
  |---|---|---:|---:|
  | d512 control, tie seed 0 / tie seed 1 / model seed 1 | random | 3.704 / 3.699 / 3.682 | 3.264 / 3.264 / 3.245 |
  | d512 ridge head | top `B` | 4.017 (+8.7%) | 3.353 (+2.9%) |
  | d512 inverted ridge head | top `B` of `-score` | 3.706 (+0.3%) | 3.513 (+7.8%) |
  | d512 longest documents | top `B` by UTF-8 bytes | 4.262 (+15.3%) | 3.871 (+18.8%) |
  | d512 shortest documents | bottom `B` by UTF-8 bytes | 3.781 (+2.3%) | 3.248 (−0.3%) |
  | d768 control | random | 3.296 | 2.791 |
  | d768 ridge head | top `B` | 3.597 (+9.1%) | 2.868 (+2.8%) |

  * changes are against the mean of the three d512 controls, or against the d768 control. a new random selection moved Paloma loss by 0.005, and a new model seed by 0.022. the d512 control is near the Hero-cache baseline (3.676)
  * each rung prefix is 10.00·B, each selection is at most one document above `B`, and the random selections have the source mix and mean ridge score of their prefix (0.6097 against 0.6095)
  * the ridge head is a domain filter: its selection has a mean score of 0.818, moves tokens from `finetranslations` and medium-quality web to PDFs, books, and synthetic QA, and improves s2orc (−7.0%) and arXiv physics (−7.6%) but not social text (Twitter +19.0%). the inverted head gives the opposite change on each of these datasets
  * the longest selection is 862 documents (mean 420k tokens, SEC filings, books, PDFs). the shortest selection is 1,223,195 documents (mean 296 tokens)
* known limits

topics.title: [shellbox] Keep ShellSim usable after command timeouts
topics.body:
The ShellSim backend closed the machine whenever one command exceeded its `command.timeout`, because the simulator's interpreter thread cannot be interrupted, and every later call then raised `Machine is closed`. In the Taskforge adversary trials of the generate-1000 run, one slow computation by the agent lost the rest of its session: 58 trials ended as unclassified and were retried to abandonment between 08:00Z and 10:00Z on 2026-10-14. Inside the simulation `sleep` costs no wall time, but CPU work does, and the wall clock does not advance, so both a heavy computation and a clock-based loop reach the timeout.

The machine now stays open, and every operation that touches the simulation is bounded by its caller's own deadline. A command with a timeout, or a shell action with a `wait`, waits for the timed-out command under the lock and runs once it ends, so two operations never run on the one-threaded simulator at once; past its own deadline it reports `TIMED_OUT` (or `RUNNING` for a shell action) and the machine stays usable. An operation with no deadline of its own, an upload, a download, or a command without a timeout, is refused at once while a timed-out command is still running, which is what those operations got before through the closed machine, and succeeds again once the command ends. A command that never ends therefore leaves the machine as unusable as before, with each later operation either timing out under its own deadline or refused immediately, never waiting without bound.

The test runs a simulated shell loop past a short timeout and checks that a transfer is refused while it runs, that a later command with a deadline completes, and that the transfer succeeds afterwards; a second test does the same through the persistent shell's `execute`. On main the first command's timeout closes the machine and both fail.

topics.title: [iris] Sandbox exec through the cw-rno2a controller saturates at ~2,000 live sandboxes
topics.body:
Shellbox's Iris backend runs every command in a sandbox, including the base64 file transfers that upload grader files, as an `ExecInContainer` RPC through the controller (`lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/iris/machine.py:92-115`; it already retries when the controller sheds an exec because its pool is full). On cw-rno2a on 2026-10-14, a Taskforge queue with about 2,150 live gVisor sandboxes (8 coordinator jobs, `/muchanem/gen1000-s*r`) saturated that path. Between 08:52 and 09:42 UTC its validation trials recorded these ungraded causes:

| Cause | Count |
|---|---|
| solver `grader_timeout` | 699 |
| solver `tool_execution` | 562 |
| control `grader_timeout` | 397 |
| build/grader-step `RolloutInterrupted` (machine start) | ~245 |
| `machine_start_timeout` | 44 |

The sandbox pods themselves were Running. An earlier read-only diagnosis of the same controller (04:30 UTC, ~1,700 sandboxes) found the controller creates pending sandbox pods only once per control tick, that the tick had grown from ~30 s to 80–160 s, and that the tick shares the controller process with all shellbox exec traffic (128 exec threads) and 64 RPC handler threads. Slow-RPC logs showed `ListTasks` at ~10.8 s and `LaunchJob` at ~12.9 s. Kubernetes, Kueue and node capacity were not the limit: a gVisor pod runs ~6 s after creation, and the cluster holds ~4,800 sandboxes at these requests.

That diagnosis also found that sandbox child jobs of a killed coordinator kept running. 52 tasks under cancelled `/muchanem/gen1000-s*n` coordinators still showed Running hours later, and their pods had to be cancelled one job at a time.

Expected: a sandbox command's latency does not grow with the number of live sandboxes on the cluster, and cancelling a coordinator ends its sandbox children.

Done when exec traffic no longer shares the controller's critical path with the control tick (an exec path that bypasses the controller, or an exec pool sized separately from the tick), and cancelling a job tears down its sandbox children.

topics.title: [levanter] Repair DPO exports and explicit-mesh sharding
topics.body:
Full-model DPO on current main has three handling gaps. First, the HF export cadence is wrong: the separate-reference export hook fires on the legacy step counter, so exports land on the wrong updates and the final update can be missed or saved twice. This registers the hook on completed optimizer updates and makes the forced final save idempotent, with the interval-final naming semantics documented.

Second, the export path cannot produce serving-ready DPO artifacts: no dtype control, no tokenizer revision pinning, an always-Auto CPU mesh that breaks explicit-mesh Snowball and MoE models, and reference-code copying that breaks on URL-like checkpoints while risking trained-weight overwrite. This adds export_dtype (bfloat16 halves artifact size), name@revision tokenizers, explicit CPU meshes for explicit-mesh models, and URL-aware code copying with unconditional weight protection; the DPO save path exports only the policy subtree since the reference copy is frozen scaffolding.

Third, explicit-mesh sharding is dropped by framework and model reshapes, breaking context-parallel training, and the jagged store returns stale slices for repeated row-0 batches. This threads sharding through each reshape (including the one-line Haliax companion the grad-accum fix depends on) and fixes the row-0 offsets.

Validation is numerical parity on explicit meshes, byte-exact export round-trips, a no-double-write cadence tripwire, and row-0 regression tests: 101 passed with 1 device-gated skip, plus both 8-device Snowball tests.

Part of #10040.

topics.title: [taskcompendium] Tell a failed grading preparation from a failed grader
topics.body:
A grading that fails while the verifier machine is being prepared, unpacking the staged archive, removing it, making the workspace, or making the reward files' directories, was recorded with the same kinds as a grader command that failed or timed out, `EXECUTION` or `TIMEOUT`, with only the message to tell them apart. A verifier deadline that expired before the grader's command ever ran was recorded as the grader timing out. A caller deciding whether a failure is the task's or the host's had nothing typed to go on. In a Taskforge generation run under a saturated cluster controller, 235 of 279 program revisions were spent on host-caused grading failures of this shape (269 deadline expiries during staging commands among them).

Two additions make the distinction typed:

- `GradingFailure.STAGING` for the runtime's own preparation commands. Commands the task's author chose, the grader's own command, its environment's setup commands and its collect commands, keep `EXECUTION` and `TIMEOUT`. The reward files' preparation moves out of the script grader's run into the staging block it belongs to, ahead of the setup commands.
- `GradingProgress`, which the sandbox grading path moves to `STAGING` before it captures the agent's output files and to `GRADER` before the first command the author chose, a setup command or the grader's own. The rollout engine, whose verifier deadline covers the preparation as well as the grader, now reports an expiry before the grader's command as `STAGING` with the error "Verifier deadline expired while preparing the verifier machine", and as `TIMEOUT` with the unchanged message otherwise. A session that grades without the sandbox path leaves the phase at `GRADER`, so nothing changes for it.

Downstream, Taskforge's validation classifier and its build-time grading will map `STAGING` to a host cause instead of a task one; that lands on its own once this is in.
