# Snowball parity-test performance on real 8×H100 nodes **Date:** 2026-07-17 · **Commit:** `4b32fcfb0747dbb83ef4c0e8a13ffa7d4863218d` · **Cluster:** `cw-us-east-02a` · **Attention:** `FLASH_ATTN` ## Summary > [!IMPORTANT] > **In this cold test path, vLLM cut end-to-end test-case time by 49% and prompt-scoring time by 8.4× relative to Levanter, while using about 10 GiB more HBM per GPU. Startup and setup—not scoring—dominated elapsed time for both backends.** | Measurement | Levanter | vLLM | Main takeaway | |---|---:|---:|---| | End-to-end test case | 535.05 s | 273.30 s | vLLM was 1.96× faster | | Model load / server startup | 334.39 s | 135.04 s | Largest phase for both backends | | Prompt scoring | 133.16 s | 15.85 s¹ | vLLM was 8.4× faster | | Peak HBM per GPU | 65,049 MiB | 75,425 MiB | vLLM used 10,376 MiB more | ¹ vLLM scoring includes an additional eight-request diagnostic. Its 64 representative requests alone took 13.05 seconds. ### Main learnings 1. **The 30-minute runtime limit has substantial observed headroom.** The slowest backend task took 8m55s, giving 3.6× headroom. The full paired pytest run passed in 13m28s. 2. **Improving cold-run latency means improving initialization.** Model loading consumed 62% of the Levanter test case. vLLM server startup consumed 49%, with another 80 seconds spent in environment setup and finalization. 3. **vLLM's performance advantage is concentrated in scoring.** The production-shaped requests took 15.85 seconds on vLLM versus 133.16 seconds on Levanter. Levanter's first batch at each shape includes JIT compilation, so these are cold test-path measurements—not a general serving benchmark. 4. **HBM is the clearest vLLM resource risk.** Its sampled peak was 92.5% of reported capacity, leaving about 6 GiB per GPU; Levanter peaked at 79.8%. ![Cold standing-cluster runtime breakdown](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/34e9ae8ab90e1e0c6d875ead0139f79ed174f102/reports/snowball-parity-runtime-2026-07-17/runtime-breakdown.png) ![Prompt scoring runtime by production-shaped batch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/34e9ae8ab90e1e0c6d875ead0139f79ed174f102/reports/snowball-parity-runtime-2026-07-17/batch-runtime.png) > [!NOTE] > **Correctness was stable on the representative set:** all 64 cases passed for both backends in the paired run, and all representative cases passed in five additional cold vLLM runs. A separate rank-consistency diagnostic was not reproducible; details are below.
Detailed performance evidence — phase timing, batching, latency, and timeout headroom The exact standing-cluster test passed for both backends on fresh 8×H100 jobs: ```text 2 passed in 808.65s (0:13:28) ``` | Backend | Pytest test case | Iris task | Remote function | Model load/startup | Prompt scoring | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Levanter | 535.05 s | 499.11 s | 485.99 s | 334.39 s | 133.16 s | | vLLM | 273.30 s | 255.38 s | 175.75 s | 135.04 s | 15.85 s¹ | ¹ vLLM scoring includes the eight-request rank diagnostic. The 64 representative requests took 13.05 seconds across eight concurrent waves; the diagnostic wave took 2.80 seconds. The 30-minute runtime limit is 3.6× the observed Levanter task duration and 7.0× the vLLM task duration. H100 assignment began 4–5 seconds after submission, so this experiment did not exercise the separate 30-minute pending limit. - The vLLM environment/setup layer took 79.63 seconds, largely from pinned CUDA 13 overlay installation and job finalization. - Levanter scored 329,514 real prompt tokens as 479,232 padded tokens (68.8% padding efficiency). - Levanter's first batch at each reused shape included JIT compilation: 15.21 vs 0.56 seconds at 256 tokens, 14.02 vs 1.39 seconds at 1,024, and 17.48 vs 4.75 seconds at 4,096. - vLLM's first short wave took 4.34 seconds and the second took 0.096 seconds, indicating first-request warmup. - Representative vLLM request latency was 0.47 seconds at the median and 4.29 seconds at the 95th percentile. ![vLLM request latency](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/34e9ae8ab90e1e0c6d875ead0139f79ed174f102/reports/snowball-parity-runtime-2026-07-17/vllm-request-latency.png)
GPU evidence — HBM, utilization, power, and temperature The monitor collected 209 complete eight-GPU samples for Levanter and 81 for vLLM at approximately two-second intervals. - Levanter peaked at 65,049 MiB per GPU, 100% utilization, 293 W, and 36°C. - vLLM peaked at 75,425 MiB per GPU, 100% utilization, 293 W, and 33°C. - Relative to the reported 81,559 MiB capacity, sampled HBM peaks were 79.8% for Levanter and 92.5% for vLLM. ![GPU resource timeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/34e9ae8ab90e1e0c6d875ead0139f79ed174f102/reports/snowball-parity-runtime-2026-07-17/gpu-resource-timeline.png)
Correctness and reproducibility — representative parity and the rank diagnostic ### What is the rank sentinel? After scoring the normal 64 representative cases, the vLLM test selects one of those same cases—`knowledge-longbench-02`, a 15,025-token prompt—and sends it eight more times, with one request pinned to each vLLM serving-rank endpoint. These eight replays are the **rank sentinel**. In plain terms, it asks whether the same long prompt produces the same probabilities regardless of which rank serves it. It is not additional golden data and does not add workload coverage. ### Result | Check | Result | Maximum probability error | Interpretation | |---|---:|---:|---| | Levanter representative set, initial paired run | 64/64 passed | `0.068273` | Passed | | vLLM representative set, five cold runs | 5/5 runs passed | `0.053180–0.067022` | Reproducible in this sample | | vLLM eight-rank sentinel, five cold runs | **2/5 runs passed** | `0.055488–0.093050` | **Not reproducible at the `0.075` gate** | The sentinel is useful as a diagnostic, but these results do not support using it as a blocking gate in its current form. #### Initial paired run | Metric | Levanter | vLLM representative | vLLM rank sentinel | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Observations | 64 | 64 | 8 | | Maximum probability error | 0.068273 | 0.060728 | **0.073430** | | Median probability error | 0.012349 | 0.011156 | 0.036522 | | 95th percentile, representative set | 0.043770 | 0.045501 | — | | Observations above the old 0.008 bound | 43 | 41 | 8 | | Supported winner changes | 5 | 5 | 0 | The sentinel initially passed, but its maximum of `0.073430` left only `0.001570` headroom under the `0.075` gate. ![Representative-case error versus prompt length](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/34e9ae8ab90e1e0c6d875ead0139f79ed174f102/reports/snowball-parity-runtime-2026-07-17/accuracy-vs-prompt-length.png) ![Initial eight-rank sentinel results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/34e9ae8ab90e1e0c6d875ead0139f79ed174f102/reports/snowball-parity-runtime-2026-07-17/vllm-sentinel-by-rank.png) #### Five cold vLLM runs Five identical tests ran concurrently on fresh 8×H100 allocations with the same commit and configuration (`FLASH_ATTN`, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, FlashInfer sampler disabled). | Run | Iris job suffix | Representative maximum | Sentinel maximum | Gate | |---:|---|---:|---:|---| | 1 | `7ff3af48` | 0.067022 | 0.074130 | pass | | 2 | `9af1f63f` | 0.053180 | 0.076045 | **fail** | | 3 | `c8ab3bb9` | 0.056067 | 0.055488 | pass | | 4 | `0373bc39` | 0.067022 | 0.093050 | **fail** | | 5 | `b3e2493b` | 0.055502 | 0.082465 | **fail** | The representative maximum stayed below the gate in every run. The high sentinel error moved between ranks rather than remaining on one consistently bad rank. ![Five-run representative and sentinel maxima](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/34e9ae8ab90e1e0c6d875ead0139f79ed174f102/reports/snowball-parity-runtime-2026-07-17/variance-5x8h100/run-maxima.png) ![Sentinel error by cold run and rank](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/34e9ae8ab90e1e0c6d875ead0139f79ed174f102/reports/snowball-parity-runtime-2026-07-17/variance-5x8h100/sentinel-error-heatmap.png) For the same sentinel rank-4/token-423 tuple, observed probability ranged from `0.475533` to `0.564618` (golden `0.557848`), a `0.089085` range. Across exact tuples, the 95th-percentile probability range was `0.010713` for representative requests and `0.043363` for sentinel requests. ![Sentinel top-token probability](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/34e9ae8ab90e1e0c6d875ead0139f79ed174f102/reports/snowball-parity-runtime-2026-07-17/variance-5x8h100/sentinel-top-token-probability.png) ![Exact-token probability ranges across runs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/34e9ae8ab90e1e0c6d875ead0139f79ed174f102/reports/snowball-parity-runtime-2026-07-17/variance-5x8h100/token-probability-range.png) The five concurrent jobs measure variation across fresh allocated nodes, not repeated execution on one fixed node. Five observations are too few for a precise failure-rate estimate, but three failures disprove reliable reproducibility at the current threshold. One original allocation (`f6b61bf9`) failed during vLLM worker initialization before scoring any request. It was replaced by run 5 and excluded from numerical analysis.
Method and limitations — commands, jobs, and telemetry effects The unmodified test contract was executed with temporary telemetry around it: ```sh uv run pytest tests/cluster/vllm/test_snowball_backend_parity.py \ -m cluster -o addopts= --import-mode=importlib -vv -s --durations=0 ``` Jobs: - Levanter: `/romain/snowball-representative-parity-levanter-8291831e` - vLLM: `/romain/snowball-representative-parity-vllm-673370df` The paired-run telemetry recorded phase, batch/wave, per-request, per-case parity, and per-GPU HBM/utilization/power/temperature. GPU polling and structured logging can perturb runtime, so timings are conservative cold-path measurements rather than a clean benchmark. Median time to emit an eight-GPU sample was below 0.3 ms for both backends; three Levanter samples had logging stalls above 0.1 seconds, with a 3.39-second maximum. The five-run follow-up used buffered per-request logprob capture and printed nothing during request serving. topics.title: [precision] QAT during SFT to ship a 4-bit-deployable EOY model
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Proposal to run **quantization-aware training during SFT / post-training** so we can ship a **natively 4-bit inference checkpoint** of our end-of-year models — the pattern Kimi K3 (MXFP4 weights + MXFP8 activations, "QAT from the SFT stage onward"), Kimi K2-Thinking (INT4 W4A16, "lossless" at ~2x decode), and Gemma-3 QAT (int4 + distillation) all use. The concrete near-term target is the checkpoint we're publishing to Hugging Face (Snowball / 67B-A2B, #7366) and the post-trained EOY MoE (#6705 / #7170); the goal is ~2x faster, ~4x smaller inference at near-BF16 quality. This issue covers **QAT-for-deployment**; making the *pretraining* matmuls run in FP4 for a training speedup is the separate, complementary native-FP4-pretraining issue #7403. Both split out of the umbrella plan #7402.

## Scope: QAT-for-deployment, not training speedup

Two things get conflated under "4-bit." This issue is only the second:

- **(A) Native low-precision training** *(sibling issue)* — the pretraining GEMMs execute in FP4 for a real ~2x speedup on Blackwell. A pretraining-cost optimization.
- **(B) QAT-for-deployment** *(this issue)* — master weights stay bf16, compute stays bf16, but **fake-quant (quantize→dequantize) ops + a straight-through estimator** are inserted during fine-tuning so the model *learns to be robust to a later low-bit deployment*. **No training speedup** — it buys inference accuracy that plain post-training quantization (PTQ) would lose.

They are independent and can both ship. This one is lower-risk and directly serves inference/serving and the HF release.

## Where Marin is today

- **Post-training runs PyTorch/CUDA**, not JAX: MarinSkyRL fork (GRPO/RLVR) and the Axolotl SFT backend fork (#6839) — the latter already carries a torchao QAT callback we don't use. Pretraining is JAX/Levanter; the framework boundary matters here because the mature FP4 QAT tooling (torchao/Axolotl) is PyTorch.
- Native in-repo SFT is Levanter-native and consolidating on a shared `sft_step` launcher (#7231, #7250, both merged) with HF↔Levanter conversion (#7337); chat-template/tool-mask correctness tracked under #7045.
- We are actively standing up the first published Marin MoE: **publish Snowball to HF** (#7366), with the first-class GrugMoE HF snapshot/loading landed in #7227 and export decoupling in #6752 — this is the checkpoint a QAT pass would produce a 4-bit variant of.
- On-policy distillation exists as a post-training mechanism (#5853, MVP in #5939), and the OPD teacher-serving RFC (#7236) already reasons about **quantization perturbing distillation targets** — directly relevant below.
- Quantization substrate is all training-side FP8/MXFP8 (#7282, #7079, #620); **no QAT-for-deployment anywhere yet.**

## What "QAT during SFT" means, and the QAT-vs-QAD distinction that matters for MoE

Keep bf16 master weights; in the SFT/post-training forward pass, fake-quantize the target tensors to the deployment grid (quantize→dequantize) so the model sees quantization noise; backprop with a straight-through estimator (rounding treated as identity) updating the bf16 masters. After training, a `convert` step packs the real low-bit checkpoint. The served weights are then natively low-bit.

The single most important finding for a **MoE that goes through SFT+RL**: plain QAT (fake-quant + task cross-entropy) can **regress below even PTQ**, because CE loss can look fine while the output distribution has drifted from the bf16 model. The fix is **QAD — quantization-aware *distillation***: replace/augment the loss with KL to the full-precision checkpoint's output distribution (teacher = the un-quantized model). Reported example (NVFP4, Nemotron MoE): PTQ AIME25 85.0, plain QAT 83.3 (worse!), **QAD 87.9** vs BF16 89.1. For an SFT-only target, QAT ≈ QAD; for our SFT+RL MoE, **use QAD**. This dovetails with our existing distillation work (#5853) and the quantized-teacher reasoning in #7236.

## Format choice

| Scheme | What | When to pick |
|---|---|---|
| **INT4 W4A16, group 32** | 4-bit weights, bf16 activations, runs on bf16 tensor cores | Kimi K2-Thinking / SGLang-slime pattern. Simplest, best train↔infer consistency, ~2x decode (bandwidth-bound), plain QAT often suffices. **Recommended default.** |
| **MXFP4 wt + MXFP8 act** | 4-bit weights + 8-bit activations, OCP MX (block 32) | Kimi K3 pattern; "broad hardware compatibility" (Hopper + Blackwell + AMD). Quantized activations add risk. |
| **NVFP4 W4A4, group 16** | 4-bit weights + activations, Blackwell-only | Max compute throughput, but activation quant needs distillation to recover; Blackwell-only serving. |

For a large MoE where decode is weight-bandwidth-bound, **W4A16 gives most of the win with the least risk**. Escalate to activation quantization only if we need the compute throughput on Blackwell serving, and pair it with QAD.

## What to quantize

Routed-expert MLP GEMMs are 90%+ of MoE params → quantize **only the routed-expert up/gate/down weights**; keep **attention (Q/K/V/O), the router/gating linear, shared/always-on experts, embeddings, LM head, and norms in BF16**. Every surveyed model does a version of this (gpt-oss: only MoE weights to MXFP4; K2-Thinking: "the MoE components"; Nemotron: last ~15% + attention + latent projections in BF16). The router especially must stay high precision — routing errors compound through expert selection.

## Recipe (concrete, from Gemma-3 / slime / NVIDIA QAD)

- **BF16 master weights + STE**; fake-quant only in the forward.
- **Full-precision warmup, then enable fake-quant** (torchao default ~1000 steps; exposed as `fake_quant_after_n_steps`) so weights stabilize before quant noise. (Kimi K3 instead runs QAT for the whole SFT.)
- **Small budget vs pretraining:** Gemma-3 used ~5000 steps; NVIDIA QAD token budgets ~0.3–3B (scaling with size; ~2.5B for a 30B-A3B MoE). Hundreds of millions to a few billion tokens.
- **Conservative LR 1e-6 → 1e-5**, at or below the original post-training LR (higher destabilizes). Distillation temperature T=1.
- **For RL rollouts:** enforce train↔infer consistency (fake-quant grid == inference grid) and consider a router-replay so expert selection matches the inference engine — Marin already has router-replay/TIS work in this area, and reuse of Grug MoE kernels in the PyTorch SkyRL trainer is tracked in #7164.
- **Evaluate with KL-to-BF16-teacher, not just task accuracy** — CE can look fine while the distribution drifts (the QAD central caution).

## Tooling: the PyTorch path, and the MoE gap

- **torchao QAT + Axolotl `qat:`** is the turnkey path and slots into our existing Axolotl SFT fork (#6839): config keys `activation_dtype` (int8/int4/float8/nvfp4), `weight_dtype` (int4/fp8/nvfp4), `group_size` (32; **16 for NVFP4**), `fake_quant_after_n_steps`; flow is `axolotl train` (torchao `QATConfig(step="prepare")`) → `axolotl quantize` (`step="convert"`). Published Blackwell NVFP4 QAT recovery: ~63–72% of degradation for Gemma3-12B/27B.
- **The gap:** torchao's mainline `FakeQuantizedLinear` targets 2D `nn.Linear`; grouped-expert 3D weight stacks / grouped-GEMM MoE are **not first-class for QAT**, and Axolotl's MoE-MXFP4 request (axolotl-ai-cloud#3333) is a closed proposal with no implementation. Kimi's own stack used a custom `_FakeInt4QuantizationSTE` inside Megatron/TransformerEngine plus `int4_block_quantize`/`pack_int4_to_int32` for export. **Expect to write MoE-expert fake-quant** rather than getting it free — verify against the installed torchao version first.
- If we want QAT inside the JAX/Levanter loop instead, note **qwix** (JAX-native QAT) supports int4/int8/fp8 but **not FP4**; a JAX MXFP4/NVFP4 fake-quant is a custom_vjp+STE build (a few hundred LOC). Since our post-training is already PyTorch, the torchao/Axolotl path is the natural fit.

## Proposed plan

- **Phase 0 — format + loss decision.** W4A16-INT4 (recommended default) vs MXFP4-W/MXFP8-A vs NVFP4-W4A4, from the serving-hardware constraint; and QAT vs QAD (QAD if the target went through RL). Decide serving target with the vLLM-fork/upstream work (#7367, #6869/#6870).
- **Phase 1 — pilot on Snowball (67B-A2B, #7366).** MoE-expert-only W4A16 QAT fine-tune with a full-precision warmup, on the PyTorch/Axolotl path; produce a packed 4-bit checkpoint, serve on the vLLM fork, measure decode speedup and accuracy vs bf16 and vs naive PTQ. This validates the MoE fake-quant plumbing on a real, already-being-published model.
- **Phase 2 — EOY post-trained MoE (#6705 / #7170).** Apply the chosen scheme (QAD if SFT+RL) as the finishing stage of post-training; ship the 4-bit checkpoint alongside the bf16 one.

## Definition of Done

- Phase 0 decisions recorded: target format (W4A16 / MXFP4-W-MXFP8-A / NVFP4) and QAT-vs-QAD, with rationale.
- MoE-expert fake-quant works in our post-training stack (torchao/Axolotl path, with custom MoE handling as needed); a natively-4-bit checkpoint of Snowball (#7366) is produced.
- Served on our vLLM fork with measured decode speedup (target ~2x vs bf16) and an accuracy-recovery number vs naive PTQ, evaluated with KL-to-BF16-teacher plus task accuracy.
- Recommendation back on #7402 on the scheme for the EOY post-trained model.

## Risks & open questions

- **Plain QAT can underperform PTQ for SFT+RL / MoE models** → default to QAD (KL to bf16 teacher) for post-RL targets; ties into #5853 / #7236.
- MoE-expert QAT is not first-class in torchao/Axolotl → budget for custom fake-quant on grouped/3D expert weights.
- Kimi K3's exact quant scope, warmup, and step budget are **undisclosed** — treat "MXFP4-W/MXFP8-A from SFT" as the target, not a reproducible recipe.
- The fake-quant grid must bit-match the deployment quantizer (torchao / our vLLM-fork kernels) or QAT trains against the wrong noise; also required for RL rollout stability.
- Serving a quantized Grug checkpoint depends on the vLLM-fork / upstream support (#7367, #6869/#6870) and export correctness (#7146).

## Prior work / related Marin issues

Umbrella plan: **#7402** (QAT & FP4 plan — parent). Sibling: **#7403** (native FP4 pretraining — regime A).

SFT infrastructure: #7045 (SFT-with-confidence umbrella), #6839 (Axolotl SFT fork — the QAT host), #7231 / #7250 (shared `sft_step`, merged), #7337 (hf→levanter), #7088 (DenseMixer router gradient for MoE SFT), #7086 / #7087 (packed-SFT masking), #7098 (post-training runnable from repo).
Post-training program: #6705 (10T post-training hero run), #7170 (first post-trained Marin MoE, 2T cut), #7074 (post-training token budget), #6053 (EOY post-training plan), #6496 (post-training data manager).
RL / SkyRL stack: #6682 (JAX backend to SkyRL), #7164 (reuse Grug MoE kernels in PyTorch SkyRL trainer), #6341 (RL feature checklist — notes quantized/AWQ teacher), #6162 (RL framework guide).
Distillation (for QAD): #5853 (on-policy distillation), #7236 (RFC: quantized-teacher serving — quantization vs distillation targets), #5939 (sampled-token OPD MVP), #6535 (self-verified distillation).
Quantized inference / serving: #7367 (upstream Grug to vLLM/HF), #6869 / #6870 (GrugMoE GPU inference), #7097 (one vLLM fork), #6136 (FP8 decode-corruption bug), #6500 (serving infra).
Publishing checkpoints: #7366 (publish Snowball to HF — Phase-1 target), #7227 (GrugMoE HF snapshot/loading, merged), #6752 (export_hf ArtifactStep), #7146 (HF RoPE export bug).
Quantization substrate (regime A, related): #7282 (MXFP8 on GB200), #620 (archived INT8/AQT).

## External references

Kimi K3 (https://www.kimi.com/blog/kimi-k3); Kimi K2-Thinking (https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Thinking) + LMSYS INT4-QAT reproduction (https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-01-26-int4-qat/); Gemma-3 QAT (https://developers.googleblog.com/en/gemma-3-quantized-aware-trained-state-of-the-art-ai-to-consumer-gpus/); NVFP4 QAD (arXiv 2601.20088); gpt-oss MXFP4 (arXiv 2508.10925); torchao QAT (https://docs.pytorch.org/ao/stable/workflows/qat.html); Axolotl QAT (https://docs.axolotl.ai/docs/qat.html) + quantize (https://docs.axolotl.ai/docs/quantize.html); Axolotl MoE-MXFP4 request (https://github.com/axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl/issues/3333); qwix (https://github.com/google/qwix).

topics.title: Build Harbor sandbox images off-slot via Cloud Build; add stress canary
topics.body:
PR #7450 builds Dockerfile-task sandbox images in-trial on the worker's own daemon (DOCKER_ACCESS sibling containers). The build occupies one of the harbor job's n_concurrent_trials slots for its full duration — up to ~8 minutes measured on apt-heavy OpenThoughts-TBLite environments — and the content-keyed tag caches per worker, so a fresh worker rebuilds. Over long eval and RL runs, slow builds form head-of-line blocking on trial slots (see the discussion on #7450).

Shape agreed in the PR discussion (rjpower, penfever):

- Resolve the dataset's full environment-hash set before opening the trial queue; the registry provides every task's environment up front.
- Dispatch missing builds to Cloud Build in parallel, pushing content-keyed tags to Artifact Registry; trials run against prebuilt images only.
- Dockerfile tasks then become ordinary prebuilt-image jobs: no DOCKER_ACCESS, no sibling machinery, the un-gated gvisor profile applies, and the k8s backend works.
- Reuse harbor's per-task environment hash if it covers file permission bits (COPY preserves them); otherwise keep the hash in marin/harbor/iris_environment.py.
- Add an intermittent stress canary measuring sandbox scheduling latency, environment-ready time, and exec round-trip (mean and tail), so any saturation-aware admission policy is grounded in measured data.

Blocked on an operator decision: Cloud Build service account (builds.editor plus AR write for the eval parent's identity) and billing.

Done when:

- A full OpenThoughts-TBLite run performs no in-trial docker builds; images build once globally and are pulled by trials on docker-worker and k8s backends.
- The stress canary runs on a schedule and reports scheduling-latency, environment-ready, and exec round-trip percentiles.

topics.title: [iris] Expose admitted topology labels for placement audits
topics.body:
## Status

This is a non-blocking observability enhancement, not a reproduced placement-correctness blocker. PR #7225 requests required and sliced topology from Kueue at admission. Recent B200 research has not shown an admitted gang violating those constraints or drifting after startup.

The reproduced gap is narrower: Iris status includes pod-to-node assignments but omits the configured topology-domain values needed to independently verify the realized placement. The probe on branch `agent/b200-repro-placement-audit` therefore returned `UNOBSERVABLE`, not `VIOLATION`.

Kueue remains the enforcement authority. This work should provide provider-independent readback and diagnostics, not act as a second scheduler or make jobs query provider APIs.

## Reproduction

Run against any admitted topology-constrained Iris gang:

    iris rpc controller get-kubernetes-cluster-status | python -m iris.cluster.topology_audit --task-prefix TASK_PREFIX --topology-key TOPOLOGY_KEY --expectation single-domain -

Current result: `UNOBSERVABLE` when the requested topology key is absent from the admitted node records.

Expected result: Iris exposes the configured topology values for admitted nodes, allowing the audit to return `MATCH`, `VIOLATION`, or `UNOBSERVABLE` for genuinely incomplete data.

## Recommended progression

### 1. Expose allowlisted realized topology

- Add a topology-label map to `NodeStatus`.
- Populate only label keys referenced by configured Kueue topology levels; do not expose every Kubernetes node label.
- Add provider-independent tests for present, missing, and partially populated labels.

This is the smallest useful increment and should be kept separate from remediation policy.

### 2. Make requested-versus-realized placement first-class

- Surface the requested topology mode, topology key, and slice size alongside the realized pod-to-node placement.
- Audit required single-domain and exact sliced placement without caller-supplied provider details.
- Return explicit `MATCH`, `VIOLATION`, or `UNOBSERVABLE` results, including enough context to diagnose a mismatch.
- Handle partial admission, retries, and missing or deleted node records without reporting false violations.

### 3. Add operational presentation if useful

- Surface the audit in the CLI or dashboard and optionally emit alerts.
- Validate it during scheduler upgrades or configuration changes.
- Consider automatic abort or retry only if violations are actually observed and an explicit policy is agreed. Automatic remediation is not part of this issue.

## Non-goals

- Replacing Kueue's admission-time enforcement.
- Hardcoding provider-specific topology labels or querying provider APIs from training jobs.
- Exposing arbitrary node labels.
- Automatically aborting jobs based on the initial audit implementation.

## Done when

Required single-domain and balanced sliced placement can be audited after admission without provider-specific API access, with requested intent and realized placement clearly distinguished.

Source: #7225
Repro branch: `agent/b200-repro-placement-audit`
Non-blocking follow-up to #6710

topics.title: [grug][EP] Preserve expert sharding through MuonH 4D Newton–Schulz
topics.body:
## Problem

At EP64, MuonH's 4D Newton–Schulz path merges `(L, E) -> LE` with `PartitionSpec(None, "data", "model")`. When `data=model=1`, this gathers and fully replicates the BF16 `[L·E,D,I]` expert stack before it can be redistributed.

## Reproduction scope

- GB200, 64-GPU expert axis
- Grug MoE: d5120, L48, E256, top-8
- MuonH with scanned 4D expert stacks
- `data=model=1`, `expert=64`
- Reproduction branch: [`rav-grug-moe-ep64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/rav-grug-moe-ep64)
- Originating result: [#7201 EP64 report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5048941489)

## Observed behavior

The merge creates a roughly 300 GiB replicated stack; the run OOMs around 310 GiB before step 1.

## Expected behavior / fix boundary

Transpose the `expert` axis to the front before merging so each shard remains contiguous and the merged value keeps an expert-sharded spec without a gather. The change should be a no-op for EP1/FSDP and allow the EP64 configuration to reach training.

## Done when

- The EP64 reproduction reaches training without this pre-step OOM.
- EP1/FSDP parity is covered.
- A focused sharding test proves no full expert-stack gather is introduced.

topics.title: [grug][EP] Shard non-expert weights and optimizer state across the expert axis
topics.body:
## Problem

Grug defines `data = devices / (replica · expert)`. At EP64 this collapses `data` to 1, so non-expert weights—attention, shared MLP, LM head—and their optimizer state are replicated on every device.

## Reproduction scope

- GB200, 64-GPU expert axis
- Grug MoE: d5120, L48, E256, top-8
- `data=model=1`, `expert=64`
- Reproduction branch: [`rav-grug-moe-ep64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/rav-grug-moe-ep64)
- Originating result: [#7201 EP64 report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5048941489)

## Observed behavior

Non-expert parameters and optimizer state consume roughly 148 GiB/GPU and OOM before step 1.

## Expected behavior / fix boundary

Use the combined FSDP axis `("data", "expert")` for non-expert weights, e.g. `P(Pfsdp, "model")` / `P("model", Pfsdp)`. The expert axis is intra-rack, so the required all-gathers remain on NVLink. At EP1 this must be equivalent to the existing `P("data", ...)` layout.

## Done when

- The EP64 reproduction reaches training without replicated non-expert-state OOM.
- EP1 retains equivalent sharding and numerics.
- Tests cover parameter and optimizer-state partition specs.

topics.title: [grug][EP] Expose ragged-all-to-all capacity factor and overflow telemetry
topics.body:
## Problem

The EP ragged-all-to-all launcher needs an explicit receive-capacity control. Without environment-driven capacity-factor plumbing, production EP64 shapes cannot size receive buffers safely or monitor token overflow consistently.

## Reproduction scope

- GB200, 64-GPU expert axis
- Grug MoE: d5120, L48, E256, top-8
- `ragged_all_to_all`, capacity factor 1.0
- Reproduction branch: [`rav-grug-moe-ep64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/rav-grug-moe-ep64)
- Originating result: [#7201 EP64 report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5048941489)

## Expected behavior

Expose `SCALE_CAPACITY_FACTOR` with default 1.0 and compute receive capacity as:

`capacity_factor × tokens_local × top_k`

Report `train/router/capacity_overflow_rate_mean` so configurations that drop tokens are visible.

## Done when

- The launcher accepts and propagates `SCALE_CAPACITY_FACTOR`.
- Default behavior remains 1.0.
- Receive-capacity sizing and overflow telemetry have focused tests.
- The EP64 reproduction runs with explicit capacity 1.0.

topics.title: Snowball 67B: vLLM DP-rank sentinel logprob variance — findings + data
topics.body:
Investigation of `test_snowball_export_matches_representative_goldens[vllm-gpu]` failing on the rank sentinel (`knowledge-longbench-02`, 15,025 tokens). Follow-up to the descriptive pass in #7354. > [!IMPORTANT] > **The gate is flaky because it asserts a quantity the stack does not hold stable.** Serving Snowball under data parallelism (8) + expert parallelism, the same prompt gets a different next-token distribution depending on which rank serves it. The divergence is created by the expert-parallel combine's **destination-dependent reduce-scatter** (~1 bf16 ulp), amplified into 0.03–0.29 probability swings by **expert-routing flips**. A deterministic combine removes it at short prompts but not long ones, and a **separate launch-scoped effect** shifts per-rank values between a few discrete states across restarts. Of three states observed, **two fail** the 0.075 bound and one passes. **How to read this.** *Findings* are our current interpretation, each with a confidence tag — `[replicated]` (holds across ≥2 launches/nodes), `[single observation]` (measured once cleanly), `[hypothesis]` (consistent with the data, not isolated by an experiment). *Evidence* (O1–O7) is the measured data, each row tied to a job you can re-pull; it is collapsed below — expand what you want to check. ## Findings 1. **At a single-chunk prompt, divergence is caused entirely by destination-dependent reduce-scatter.** `[replicated]` — The production collective returns 8 different results for one identical sum, reproducibly and across nodes (O4); at 128 tokens the first MoE combine is where 8 identical inputs become 8 different outputs (O5); making the combine deterministic removes that divergence entirely (O6, O7). Ring reduce-scatter sums each destination's chunk in a rank-rotated order and rounds on the bf16 store. 2. **The amplifier is expert routing.** `[single observation]` — A ~1 ulp perturbation flips the router's top-4 by layer 14 and reaches 5 distinct expert sets by layer 25 (O5). A rounding difference cannot move a probability by 0.1; a change in *which experts run* can. Seen at 128 and 2,048, characterised in full only at 128. 3. **A deterministic combine is necessary but not sufficient.** `[replicated]` — It removes the first-layer divergence and 85% of the 128-token spread, but as little as 5% at 15,025 (O6), because multi-chunk prefills also diverge *upstream* of the combine. 4. **A second, chunk/position-dependent divergence sits in the local path, upstream of the combine.** `[single observation]` — Two single-job signatures: at 2,048 the pre-dispatch hidden is already split across ranks before any combine (O5), and with the combine made deterministic the terminal gathered-batch position is the only rank that still differs (O7). The responsible kernel is not identified. 5. **Launch-to-launch movement is a separate, discrete mechanism.** `[replicated]` fact / `[hypothesis]` cause — Per-rank values recur to six decimals across jobs, nodes, and days (O3): discrete, not drift, and not the collective (whose per-rank output is launch-invariant). *What* varies at launch is unidentified; cold-vs-warm compile/autotune is the obvious guess but does not fit cleanly. 6. **The gate samples an unstable quantity.** `[replicated]` — Identical config yields ≥3 states, 2 failing (O2). The 64-case wave scores each case on one rank and is stable; the sentinel replays across all 8 ranks, so its verdict depends on the draw. This is the flakiness in #7354. > [!NOTE] > **Proposed direction (not yet filed).** A deterministic combine alone will not make the gate reliable (finding 3), and both GPU backends already sit ~0.055 below the TPU golden here for unrelated reasons, leaving ~0.02 of headroom — smaller than the launch movement. The change that lands in this repo is a **test-contract change**: keep the 64-case golden assertion, replace the sentinel's cross-rank golden assertion with a same-rank determinism check (which held 5/5, O1), and log rank spread rather than asserting it. Separately, the collective and kernel behaviours (O4, O7) are candidate upstream vLLM issues. ## Evidence (measured)
O1 — Per-rank output is deterministic and context-invariant Fresh recomputes (caching off, cache reset between) are **bitwise identical**: 8/8 repeats at 15,025 and 8,192 tokens in the full session, 4/4 in each other session. Per-rank values are also bit-identical across isolated replay, concurrent waves (2 rounds), a staggered wave (~200 ms offsets), reverse and random service order, and a wave-realistic composition (sentinel on one rank, seven different long prompts on the others; Δ = 0.000000 for the sentinel-carrying rank in all 4 rounds).
O2 — Rank spread and gate verdict, by launch (2 of 3 states fail) Five launches produced three distinct states (S2/S3/S4 are one state; S2 and S3 are bit-identical): | session | S @ 15,025 | S @ 8,192 | worst-vs-golden @ 15,025 | vs 0.075 | |---|---|---|---|---| | S1 (first launch in job) | 0.111884 | 0.234087 | 0.098835 | **fail** | | S2 | 0.071126 | 0.286958 | 0.070121 | pass | | S3 (bit-identical to S2) | 0.071126 | 0.286958 | 0.070121 | pass | | S4 (caching on, gate-exact order) | 0.071126 | — | 0.070121 | pass | | XJ (second job, second node) | 0.099165 | 0.221011 | 0.078494 | **fail** | At 8,192 the greedy token itself differs across ranks in every session (ranks return 423 or 426). Three additional long prompts (23,113 / 14,734 / 11,291 tokens) also show cross-rank disagreement, two with the greedy token differing — so this is not specific to the sentinel. Spread is not monotone in length, and the sentinel's length is not the worst case. S1, left-truncated sentinel: | tokens | 128 | 2,048 | 8,192 | 15,025 | |---|---|---|---|---| | S1 spread | 0.041857 | 0.039831 | **0.234087** | 0.111884 | It peaks at 8,192 (16 prefill chunks) and 2,048 is as low as 128. The session ranking also flips with length: at 8,192, S2/S3 (0.286958) > S1 (0.234087) > XJ (0.221011), the reverse of their order at 15,025.
O3 — Launch movement recurs bit-exactly across jobs, nodes, days Per-rank |Δp|: S2→S3 (same job/node) = **0.000000**; S1→S2 = 0.046777 @ 15,025 (0.301409 @ 8,192); S2→XJ (different job/node) = 0.026833 @ 15,025 (0.278763 @ 8,192). The per-rank values are not drifting — they recur exactly. Rank 0 at 8,192 tokens: | launch | p(423) | |---|---| | XJ (`crossjob-d7c849b9`) | 0.621766 | | earlier job `snowball-experiment-b-vllm-bd7f6354` (day before) | 0.621766 | | S2 / S3 (`main-b20426d2`) | 0.343003 | | earlier job `snowball-experiment-b-vllm-de845a00` | 0.343003 | XJ also matched `bd7f6354` on ranks 1, 3 and 6.
O4 — The collective returns 8 different results for one identical sum Model-free reproducer on the production expert-parallel communicator; all 8 destinations receive the same mathematical sum. Equal-sizes dense mode, all sessions: | operand scale | distinct checksums (8 dest) | bit-stable over 16 iters | max \|out − fixed-order fp32 ref\| | mismatched elements | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 8 | yes | 1.25e-01 | 684,812 / 1,310,720 (52%) | | 8 | 8 | yes | 1.0 | 684,812 | | 32 | 8 | yes | 4.0 | 684,812 | Max deviation scales exactly with operand magnitude (1× → 8× → 32×), i.e. ≤1 bf16 ulp per element. The 4-of-8-sparse and uneven-sizes modes give the same picture (sparse: 431,924 mismatched). The eight per-rank checksums are **identical in S1, S2, S3, and XJ (different node)**, and all three fixed-order fp32 reference orderings (rank order, reversed, ring-rotated) agree bitwise with each other — so a fixed-order fp32 combine is destination-independent by construction.
O5 — Boundary trace: where the ranks first diverge Each serving rank's own prefill is compared across the 8 serving ranks; distinct values, 1 = all agree. The gathered-batch boundary (`b2`) differs by construction — each rank's real tokens sit at a different offset — so the informative boundaries are `b1` (input to the MoE) and `b5` (output of the combine). **128 tokens (single prefill chunk, 26 MoE calls):** | MoE call | b1 pre-dispatch | b5 post-combine | distinct top-4 expert sets | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | **1** | **8** | 1 | | 2–13 | 8 | 8 | 1 | | 14 | 8 | 8 | **3** | | 25 | 8 | 8 | **5** | At 128, everything before the first MoE is bitwise identical on all 8 ranks (b1 call 1 = 1); the first combine turns 8 identical inputs into 8 different outputs. **2,048 tokens (4 prefill chunks, 104 MoE calls):** | MoE call | b1 pre-dispatch | b5 post-combine | |---|---|---| | 1 | **2** | 8 | | 2+ | 8 | 8 | At 2,048 the pre-dispatch hidden is **already 2-distinct at the first MoE** — ranks 3,4 versus the other six — *before any combine*. A multi-chunk prefill therefore carries a rank-dependent difference upstream of the combine, on top of the combine's own 8-way split. The 3,4 grouping does not match the 4+4 PCI-socket split, and it is absent at 128.
O6 — Intervention: a destination-independent combine (−85% at 128, −5…−57% long) All-gather every rank's partial, sum in rank order in fp32, slice this rank's chunk. Measured B–A–A–B in one server, two launches. `baseline_pre` reproduces `baseline_post` bit-exactly; the two treatment sweeps reproduce each other bit-exactly. | length | F1 baseline → treatment | F2 baseline → treatment | |---|---|---| | 128 | 0.042688 → 0.006272 (−85%) | 0.042688 → 0.006272 (−85%) | | 8,192 | 0.200678 → 0.171888 (−14%) | 0.270564 → 0.157229 (−42%) | | 15,025 | 0.066786 → 0.063381 (−5%) | 0.080416 → 0.034474 (−57%) | At 15,025 in F1 the treatment moved the sentinel *further* from the golden (worst-vs-golden 0.066453 → 0.085918): better-conditioned arithmetic is not the same as agreement with a cross-hardware golden.
O7 — Trace with the intervention installed (residual is one rank) Same per-rank trace at 128 tokens, fixed combine active: | MoE layer | post-combine distinct | grouping | |---|---|---| | 1 | **1** | all 8 ranks identical | | 2 | **2** | ranks 0–6 identical, rank 7 alone differs | | 3+ | 2 | ranks 0–6 identical, rank 7 alone differs | Rank 7 is the terminal position in the gathered batch. The GPUs split 4+4 by PCI bus id, which does not match the 7-vs-1 grouping — pointing to a tile/padding boundary in the local kernel, not the collective.
Setup — exact serving config and instrumentation 67B-A2B MoE, 256 experts, top-4, 32 experts/rank, 26 layers, bf16. Served exactly as the gate does: `--data-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel --max-num-seqs 1 --max-num-batched-tokens 512`, FlashAttention, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, `VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0`. Prefix caching off in all arms except the gate-exact session S4. Fork `afb2671946`. Per-rank internals were read from live servers via vLLM's `--worker-extension-cls` mixed into the Worker and called through `POST /collective_rpc` (`VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1`); bulk data went to a node-local dir, not the RPC response. Metrics: **S** = spread (max−min) across the 8 ranks of the probability of a fixed token; **worst-vs-golden** = the gate's own statistic, max over the golden's 25 tokens of |p_observed − p_golden|, bound 0.075.
Corrections to earlier claims in this investigation (negative results) Recorded so they don't mislead future work. We first reported position sensitivity as *falsified*, because isolated/concurrent/staggered modes gave bit-identical outputs (O1). The trace (O5) showed why that inference was wrong: **vLLM serialises these requests** — the DP size vector during a "concurrent" wave is `[1,…,128,…,1]`, one real chunk and seven dummy tokens — so none of those modes varied gathered-batch position. O1 establishes that timing/peer-content/service-order are irrelevant *given* that scheduling; it says nothing about position. Our first boundary-trace design was invalid for the same reason and was discarded (job `trace-4e8f82aa`).
Data, reproduction & audit — jobs, R2 archive, audit recipe Full raw blocks are in finelog (per-task stdout), retrievable with `iris job logs /romain/`: | job | role | |---|---| | `snowball-experiment-c-main-b20426d2` | O1–O5 (4 sessions + gate-exact) | | `snowball-experiment-c-crossjob-d7c849b9` | O2–O4 cross-job/node band | | `snowball-experiment-c-trace-e15f0c4e` | O5 boundary trace | | `snowball-experiment-c-fixedcombine-2b0db3ad` | O6 intervention | | `snowball-experiment-c-tracefixed-5d61f23f` | O7 residual trace | Those logs are archived to Cloudflare R2 at `s3://marin-na/finelog/cw-us-east-02a` (the `iris job logs` path reads from that archive; the cluster's 250 GB local disk is only the ingest buffer), so the raw data outlives any single node. To audit any table above, pull a job's blocks and recompute from source: ``` iris job logs /romain/snowball-experiment-c-main-b20426d2 > main.log uv run python tests/cluster/vllm/_experiment_c_analyze.py main.log ``` `_experiment_c_analyze.py` recomputes every table from the raw `EXPERIMENT_C_JSON` blocks, so the raw → table step is inspectable code, not a hand-transcription. The reduced fixture that regenerates the tables offline (`_experiment_c_reduce_fixture.py`) is measurement data and is not committed; regenerate it from the logs on demand. The probe, harness, analyzer, and reducers are on branch [`rank-variance-g1-harness`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/rank-variance-g1-harness/tests/cluster/vllm), with the fuller root-cause report and gated plan under `docs/reports/` and `.agents/projects/` on the same branch. Two earlier jobs (`main-c13d5d45`, `crossjob-2f72ea73`) failed at startup on a probe defect and produced no data. The earlier descriptive pass (Experiments A/B: the length ladder, the Levanter-GPU head-to-head, and the golden-token deltas that O3's recurrence values come from) is summarized in the report `docs/reports/snowball-gpu-golden-logprob-parity.md`; its raw blocks are in jobs `snowball-experiment-b-{vllm-bd7f6354,vllm-de845a00,levanter-9f283c4b}`.

topics.title: [vLLM] Diagnose Snowball TPU long-context logprob divergence
topics.body:
Snowball 67B served through TPU-vLLM differs from native Levanter TPU at long
context. Three clean v6e-8 processes produced bitwise-identical observations
for all 64 representative prompts, with complete selected-token coverage and no
nonfinite values or router overflows. Maximum probability errors against the
native TPU golden were:

| Context bucket | Maximum error | Greedy agreement |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 256 | 0.030292 | 16/16 |
| 1K | 0.044239 | 14/16 |
| 4K | 0.082621 | 16/16 |
| 16K | 0.586413 | 3/8 |
| 32K | 0.436956 | 4/8 |

The qualified path used vLLM
`b66e4159789e09a87ce0b9e8bf679c46bb78ffe8`, tpu-inference
`88674e89b2fa120622448fe06ed00ae5e9b1faef`, TP8/DP1, and a top-4096
diagnostic response.

#7554 records related GPU long-context sensitivity, but the measured mechanisms
are different. Its GPU path uses DP8/expert parallelism and varies by rank and
launch. This TPU path uses DP1 and repeated bitwise across processes and slices.
MoE routing may amplify low-level numerical differences in both paths; a common
root cause has not been established.

The TPU parity PR will retain all 64 prompts under compatibility-smoke bounds of
0.04/0.05/0.10/0.70/0.50. These bounds prevent regression but do not claim
strong 16K/32K numerical parity.

Done when: identify the first material TPU-vLLM/native-TPU divergence at 16K and
32K, determine whether it shares a mechanism with #7554, and either reduce the
long-context envelope or document why the remaining difference is expected.

topics.title: [iris] Finish the operator vocabulary and resource-model cleanup
topics.body:
Follow-on to #7543 and PR #7546. #7543 landed the incident-driven vertical slice — a read-only operator CLI without provider extras, `task`/`attempt describe`, and persisted per-attempt backend identity plus a bounded terminal reason, so a past failed-in-init attempt self-explains after its pod is gone. This issue tracks the rest of the uniform noun-verb vocabulary and the internal resource-model cleanup.

Design and rationale live in `.agents/projects/2026-07-23_iris_operator_vocabulary.md` on PR #7546, including the codex peer review (request-changes) folded into its "Peer review response" section. Delivery is one design, several PRs, incident slice first.

## Landed on PR #7546
- [x] Read-only operator CLI without `iris[controller]` (lazy `CloudK8sService`)
- [x] `task describe` / `attempt describe`
- [x] Persist per-attempt pod name/uid/node + bounded terminal reason (migration 0047)

## Part I — finish the CLI vocabulary
- [ ] `DescribeTask` RPC: live enrichment (phase, live init-container status, node) for a running or pending attempt, returning a typed partial-result so `GetTaskStatus` stays a cheap poll
- [ ] `spec` verb: `job spec` / `task spec` over `GetJobStatus.request`, presented as a sanitized submitted configuration (the request is redacted, so not a guaranteed re-runnable spec). Making it genuinely reproducible is a submission-model change designed in #7565 (secret + bundle references)
- [ ] `events` verb — blocked on the events design decision below
- [ ] `stop` rework — blocked on the stop design decision below
- [ ] Renames and matrix fill: `job summary`→`describe`, `cluster status`→`describe`, `slice`/`worker` promotion, `endpoints`→`endpoint`, `process` dissolution; prune the cells the review showed are unimplementable (actor list/describe/events, attempt profile, task/cluster spec)
- [ ] Package restructure: one module per noun over a shared render/targets layer
- [ ] Write the vocabulary into `lib/iris/OPS.md`; sweep skills and docs to the new verbs

## Part II — internal resource model
- [ ] Extract a minimal typed `ResourceKey` (plus `AttemptLocator`/`AttemptIdentity`); share the target/source/`JobName` parsing behind adapters. No full `ResourceRef` subsumption and no generic `List(kind, query)`.
- [ ] Mechanical renames (no behavior change): fold the `vm` proto noun into worker/slice; rename `platforms/vm_lifecycle.py` → `controller_lifecycle.py`; split the CLI grab-bags; align the controller-side stop vocabulary (`kick_tasks`/`terminate_job`/`Worker.KillTask`); make the shared CPU-sampling helper public; optionally split the 3.5k-line `service.py`
- [ ] Docstring sweep to the `reads.py` convention; drop `__all__` blocks that only mirror the import list
- [ ] Schema alignment (migration-gated, last): typed state adapters over an int→string migration; name the three event streams by role without renaming established namespaces; decide the free-floating ids (`backend_id`/`scale_group`/`user_id`/`cluster`) per coordinate; pick the `slice`↔`worker` denormalization direction after measuring real DBs

## Cross-cutting (thread through Parts I and II)
- [ ] Federation: a home cluster and, where different, an execution cluster on every ref and event; proxy to the authoritative peer or return a structured partial for describe/events/stop
- [ ] Authorization: per-resource tenant authz before any DB/finelog/backend read; redaction allowlists for event details and backend messages; principal identity on stop/audit events; terminal-control-character sanitization
- [ ] Versioning: proto field/RPC deploy order and capability detection; a precise replacement message for any removed command
- [ ] Performance/isolation: no per-task live GET in `job describe` unless requested; no event queries on the control thread; deadlines and backend rate limits on live describes

## Open design questions (block `events` and `stop`)
1. **events** — finelog namespace and durability contract (audit vs telemetry), the event schema (id, provenance, parent keys), retention, and drop/backpressure behavior.
2. **stop** — distinct domain verbs (`cancel`/`retry`/`terminate`/`delete`) versus one overloaded `stop`; asynchronous accepted-vs-completed semantics; an `attempt_uid` compare-and-stop to close the attempt-rollover race.

topics.title: [iris] Reproducible job spec via secret and bundle references
topics.body:
## Problem

The `spec` verb (#7560) should render the definition a job was submitted with, sufficient to resubmit. It cannot be faithful today, for two structural reasons in the submission model.

**Secrets are inline literals.** Per-job env — `HF_TOKEN`, `WANDB_API_KEY`, every `-e KEY VALUE` — is carried as literal values end to end: the client injects them from its shell into `EnvironmentConfig.env_vars` (a `map<string,string>`, `rpc/job.proto:427`; `cluster/types.py:744`), the controller persists them verbatim in `job_config.environment_json` (`controller/schema.py`), and the k8s backend writes them straight into each pod's container env (`backends/k8s/tasks.py:619`). The only redaction is a cosmetic read-side copy in `get_job_status` (`cluster/redaction.py:40`, `controller/service.py:1789`). So a rendered spec must either leak the secrets or redact them into something that will not re-run. Separately, the plaintext already sits at rest in the controller DB and in every pod manifest (`kubectl get pod -o yaml`).

**Bundles render by id only.** `reconstruct_launch_job_request` rebuilds the request from normalized columns and drops `bundle_blob` (only `bundle_id` survives), along with `container_profile`, `client_revision_date`, and `federation` (`controller/codec.py:148`). A spec is a reference to a bundle, so its reproducibility depends on that bundle still existing.

## Proposal

Move secrets and bundles from inline values to named references that iris resolves, so a spec becomes a manifest of references with no secret material to redact.

### Secrets: reference, delegate the store

Submit `env_vars` values as references (`iris-secret://…`, or the existing `gcp-secret://…`) and resolve them at run time. iris already has the resolver: `rigging.secrets` resolves `env:` / `file:` / `gcp-secret://` (`secrets.py:33`), used today for cluster-config fields (`oauth_client_secret`, `signing_key`) behind an `assert_no_inlined_secrets` deploy guard (`cluster/config.py:113,1123`). Extending that resolver to per-job env is the natural step.

Two constraints:
- **Delegate the store.** iris resolves references; GCP Secret Manager and k8s Secrets hold the material. iris does not become a vault (encryption at rest, rotation, ACLs, audit) — that surface already exists in the cloud providers.
- **Resolve at the workload.** The pod resolves its own references (workload identity → Secret Manager, or a projected k8s Secret, as the `iris-task-env` envFrom already does — `backends/k8s/tasks.py:684`), so the literal never lands in the DB or the manifest. Controller-side resolution would restore reproducibility but keep the plaintext-in-manifest exposure.

This ties into per-tenant authorization (a cross-cutting item on #7560): a job may resolve only the references its tenant is cleared for.

### Bundles: formalize the reference, fix the lifetime

A bundle is already a SHA-256 content address (`cluster/bundle.py:33`): the controller stores it at `gs://…/bundles/{sha256}`, persists the id durably in `job_config.bundle_id` (`controller/schema.py:301`), and re-fetches it at dispatch via `{controller}/bundles/{id}.zip` (`backends/k8s/bundle_fetch.py:52`). An `iris-bundle://<hash>` scheme would formalize that content id into a self-describing URI — useful for spec portability, cosmetic on its own.

The substantive gap is lifetime, and it is the direct cause of the #7542 job loss. Nothing pins the bytes to a referencing job: the DB keeps the hash indefinitely, but the GCS object is TTL-expired (smoke/CI state roots under `tmp/ttl=7d/…`, `cli/cluster.py:548`) or wiped by `--clear-state` (`cli/cluster.py:562`), after which the `stage-workdir` init container 404s against a live id (`controller/dashboard.py:597`). **This half is independently shippable and does not depend on the rest of this design:** pin bundle bytes to referencing job records (ref-count, or exempt the `bundles/` prefix from TTL while a job references it). It should be pulled into its own PR as the concrete fix for the incident.

## Reproducibility semantics

A spec of references reproduces only where the references resolve: same secret project, a live bundle object, the correct controller. That matches every CI and Kubernetes manifest. `spec` should present as a manifest of references and surface per-reference resolvability, so an old spec whose bundle was collected fails loudly.

## Resolution seam

Custom schemes register through fsspec (`register_implementation` plus an `AbstractFileSystem` subclass, the `mirror://` pattern — `rigging/filesystem/mirror.py`), and iris already does I/O through raw `fsspec.core` (`cluster/bundle.py:52`), so a bundle scheme is reachable there. Secret resolution is a name→value lookup; `rigging.secrets` already handles it, so a scheme string can front it.

## Sequencing

1. Ship `spec` now over the reconstructed request with an explicit caveat (env redacted, bundle by id, not guaranteed re-runnable).
2. Pin bundle bytes to referencing jobs — standalone, closes the #7542 root cause.
3. Per-job secret references resolved at the workload; retire the redaction and the plaintext-at-rest exposure; `spec` drops its caveat.
4. Optional `iris-bundle://` / `iris-secret://` URI formalization and per-reference resolvability in `spec`.

## Open questions

- Scheme surface: reuse `gcp-secret://` directly, or front it with `iris-secret://` for backend independence?
- Bundle lifetime mechanism: DB ref-count versus a TTL exemption on referenced objects; who decrements on job GC?
- Resolution failure semantics: hard-fail the task on an unresolvable reference (as bundle fetch does today) with a typed reason surfaced through `describe`.
- Migration: env values that look secret keep working via the inline path until submitters move to references; a deploy-time guard rejects new inline secrets once references exist.

Follow-on to #7560 (the `spec` verb) and the closed #7543. The bundle-lifetime item is the root-cause fix for #7542. Design note for review; no code yet.

topics.title: [iris] Deferred configmap and PDB cleanup is lost on controller restart
topics.body:
Configmap and PDB cleanup for a killed or swept task is deferred through `_pending_gc_hashes`, which lives only in the controller process. A restart drops it, and nothing rescans, so those configmaps and PDBs stay in etcd for good. After a large backlog drain the set holds thousands of hashes whose pods are already deleted, which is exactly when the record is least reproducible: the pods that named those hashes are gone, so no later pass can derive them again.

All three producers now feed that one set — the stray-pod kill path, the gang sweep, and (since #7882) the age sweep. Before #7882 the age sweep deleted inline, so a restart lost less; inline deletion had its own permanent-orphan failure mode, which is why it was moved.

There is no orphan scan anywhere: the only `CONFIGMAPS` delete left in `tasks.py` is the label-selector delete in step 1 of the GC pass, driven entirely by that set.

Done when:
- A configmap or PDB whose task has no pod in any phase, and which is older than `_GC_MAX_AGE_SECONDS`, is reclaimed without depending on process memory.
- The age guard is explicit: `_apply_pod` writes the configmap before the pod exists, so a young configmap with no pod is a task starting up, not an orphan.
- A test covers a hash enqueued, the provider replaced (simulating restart), and the resources still reclaimed.

comments.body:
Hi! I would like to take this one, if nobody is working on it yet. I already have a fix with tests on my branch: [konstde00/marin@e463eed](https://github.com/konstde00/marin/commit/e463eedb9615fd22a03593f99a7ac137ccec99af) (based on [`ba26735`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/ba26735609dd23622ad125f4b49dd7bc5efd936f)).

I think the problem is a bit bigger than restarts. After restart everything in `_pending_gc_pods` is lost, yes, but some pods never get into this queue at all. For example, [Kueue deletes the pods it evicts](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ba26735609dd23622ad125f4b49dd7bc5efd936f/lib/iris/docs/task-states.md?plain=1#L199), and the same happens with a pod apply that fails after the ConfigMap and PDB were created, or with the output-finalization timeout, which force-deletes the pod. So persisting the queue alone won't help much.

What I did is a sweep in the GC thread: it looks for Iris ConfigMaps and PDBs older than the 1-hour age guard whose pod doesn't exist anymore, and deletes them by exact name (same as [the retry cleanup change](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9705)). The queue is still used as the fast path.

<details>
<summary>How I tested it</summary>

- New test that restarts the provider after a pod was deleted - fails on main, passes with the fix.
- Crash at each step of one attempt on the in-memory fake (14 cases): objects leak in 4 cases on main, 0 with the fix.
- kind, `kill -9` of the provider with 20 tasks waiting for cleanup: on main all 20 ConfigMaps and 20 PDBs were still there after 240 s, with the fix the first GC pass deleted all 40.
- kind, `kubectl delete pod --force`: on main both objects stayed, with the fix nothing was left.
- All 424 k8s backend tests pass with the fix.
</details>

The sweep runs on the first GC pass after start and then every 10 minutes - the objects it deletes are older than an hour anyway, so running it more often doesn't make much sense. It deletes max 500 objects per run, so a big backlog won't block the GC thread for long. Both numbers are more or less a guess, so feel free to suggest other values.

One more thing about "Done when" - I suggest to check "no pod with the name derived from the object's name, in any phase" instead of "whose task has no pod". PDBs select pods by task hash, so an old attempt's PDB would also select the retry's pod, and Kubernetes can't evict a pod which is selected by 2 PDBs.

topics.title: [grug] Count sliding-window attention in base MoE MFU
topics.body:
Count sliding-window attention when reporting model FLOP utilization (MFU) for the base MoE template. The previous calculation treated every layer as full attention and overstated MFU when the window was shorter than the sequence.

Use the same layer schedule for the forward pass and the FLOP estimate. Every fourth layer and the final layer use full attention. All other layers use the configured sliding window. Pass the full-attention layer count explicitly to include the final layer when the total depth is not divisible by four.

The compute-budget heuristic retains its full-attention convention because its learning-rate and batch-size fits use that convention. This change corrects reported FLOPs without changing training configurations or model outputs.

topics.title: [datakit] Register the hero quality data as Datakit steps
topics.body:
Register the hero quality data as two Datakit steps and make the store-ready
dataset a StepSpec output. `bucket.quality_step` reads three co-partitioned leaves
of a source (the normalized shard for row order, the fusion score leaf, and the
content-type leaf), applies the per-type calibration, and writes one shard per
basename with `source`, `id`, `content_type`, `raw_score`, `score` and
`quality_bucket` in the normalized row order. Its artifact is the `QualityScores`
the store already consumes, so `build_clustered_store` reads it unchanged.
`hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity, and `run.py --stage bucket`
produces it for every registered source.

`score_fusion.fusion_score_step` is the producer of record for the raw scores,
and follows the data flow #9694 gave the reference quality step: one Zephyr task
per shard on GPU workers reads each document's first 512 stored `input_ids` from
the source's Nemotron tokenize leaf (`iter_tokenized_documents` regroups chunk
rows) in lockstep with the normalized shard's ids, and the Harrier embedding by
position. No tokenizer runs on the worker. The step depends on the tokenize step
(`hero_data.tokenize_step_for(source, NEMOTRON_TOKENIZER)`), refuses a tokenize
artifact built from another normalize output or tokenizer repository before it
lists anything, and carries the tokenizer commit in its identity twice: through
the tokenize dependency's hash and through the pin. The Nemotron tokenize leaves
the August 14 run read were deleted from S3 after it, so the run's scores are
registered by path map as `hero_data.fusion_scores` rather than rescored; a
rerun of the score stage tokenizes the source again (the runner builds the
dependency) and lands at the step's own identity. The content-type leaves
written beside those scores are registered the same way as
`hero_data.content_type`, and `hero_data.harrier` now returns a frozen step so the
score step can depend on it.

Every input leaf of a source holds the normalized shard's documents in its row
order. A census over all 162,535 shards of the 292 sources found every
fusion-score, content-type and Harrier shard in exactly the normalized order, with
the same ids and row counts. Both steps therefore read their side inputs by
position and check each batch's ids against the normalized shard
(`AlignedColumn` for whole-column sides, `AlignedDocuments` for the streamed
tokenize side), so a leaf from a different normalize run fails its shard.
`QualityScores.samples_output_dir` is removed; the stage report reads its
spot-check text from the normalized shard of the same basename, and the reference
quality step from #9694 keeps its lockstep tokenize/normalize read without the
samples side output.

The model directory moves to `datakit/models/quality/nemotron_88k`, relative to
`MARIN_PREFIX`, with the config fields of the removed bigram, MoE, frozen-donor
and dtype arms dropped from `model.py` and the saved meta. `load_pooled_scorer`
resolves the artifact stem from the directory, so the token-window `PooledScorer`
from #9694 loads both `pooled_junkgate2_marin` and `nemotron_88k`. `QualityPin`
carries separate digests for the scorer artifacts and the calibration file,
checked by the worker before it writes, so a refit calibration moves the bucketed
dataset without moving or rescoring the raw scores. The calibration file parses
into a `Calibration` dataclass (global or per-type curves); `calibrate_model`
from #9694 writes it. Manifest entries for `harrier`, `fusion_scores`,
`content_type` and `quality` cover all 292 sources. The fusion checkpoint's
document-embedding weights form one optional `DocFusion` submodule whose field
order matches the serialized leaves, so the deployed checkpoint loads to identical
weights and scores.

The bucket stage has run over all 292 sources: 18,710,478,349 documents in
162,535 shards, equal to the fusion-score totals, in 2h50m with 12 sources in
flight on CPU workers. On `nsf_awards` (3 shards, 381,789 documents) the output
reproduced the normalized row order, the pinned raw scores and content types, and
the calibrated buckets on every row. The score stage was rerun on `nsf_awards`
from the tokenize leaf (Iris job `/muchanem/hero-quality-score-smoke-nsf`:
tokenize under Nemotron, then score against the pinned Harrier embeddings) and
matched the pinned scores row for row, same ids and order, to a maximum
difference of 1.56e-3 (mean 2.28e-4), the bf16 reduction-order noise of a
4,096-document batch against the earlier 32,768. A local end-to-end test runs
`score_fusion` over hand-written tokenize and embedding leaves with a tiny fusion
model and checks order, window truncation, chunk regrouping and the refusals.

topics.title: [eval] Resume existing Harbor runs for selective recovery
topics.body:
Resume an existing Harbor evaluation with `--resume-run-id`, then optionally retry its unscored trials with `--retry-unscored-harbor-trials`. The launcher reads the saved record and reuses the original run ID and results directory instead of creating an empty output tree.

Recovery requires one Harbor evaluation with the original model, hosted judge, policy, runtime, and version. The current error taxonomy preserves scored outcomes, including zero-reward agent failures, and leaves unknown errors available for diagnosis. A launcher regression covers persisted results, selective recovery, and rejection of a changed checkpoint under the same model name.

Resume only after the original Iris group and any earlier retry have ended. A saved record can be stale while a retry is running, so the launcher cannot detect concurrent drivers from the record alone. Missing-record errors identify the selected prefix and point to the platform, accelerator, and records-prefix controls.

Fixes #9100

topics.title: [zephyr] Let shutdown() cancel a running execute() or start()
topics.body:
A dedicated pool that execute() starts is registered with the context before
any wait, and shutdown() stops registered pools before it takes the state lock.
An execute() blocked on its coordinator or first worker now returns promptly
with ZephyrContextClosed. So does a start() blocked in the same place, which
previously also blocked shutdown() behind the state lock start() holds.

Cancellation is terminal. shutdown() sets a closing flag together with the
registry sweep, so a cancelled execute() raises instead of entering the retry
loop and launching a fresh pool, and an execute() on a shared pool reports the
error it sees after shutdown() as ZephyrContextClosed. shutdown() on a context
that never started a pool closes it instead of returning as a no-op, so a later
execute() raises rather than starting work nobody will collect.
ZephyrContextClosed subclasses RuntimeError, which the closed-context check
already raised.

Before #7145 execute() kept its coordinator job on the instance and shutdown()
terminated it from any thread; the shared-pool rewrite dropped that without a
replacement. On 2026-08-22 a driver could not cancel execute() calls whose
v5litepod workers never scheduled, and each held its thread until the 12-hour
worker wait expired.

The Iris group wait fails fast once its job is cancelled, so stopping the pool
is what releases the wait and the coordinator is unchanged. An execute() whose
pipeline is already running is released on Iris when the coordinator job is
cancelled; under LocalClient the in-process coordinator outlives its registry
entry and finishes its in-flight task drain (up to 300 s) first. The regression
tests cover the two blocked-wait cases under LocalClient with a fake worker
group that mirrors the Iris fail-fast; the Iris path itself is reasoned from
iris_backend.py and still needs a cluster run to confirm.

Fixes #8594

topics.title: [grug] Add the H100 pipeline foundation
topics.body:
Add a stage-local JAXPP pipeline for the full MoE model blocks, including latent/shared experts, SConv, attention positions and QB routing. Standard 1F1B remains the default. The synthetic runner supports the main recipe with FP32 parameters, BF16 compute and compute-scaled MuonH; the historical BF16 capacity recipe remains available.

Each routed expert parameter bank now shares one Frobenius norm across its experts, matching the stacked EP model. `--expert-normalization per_expert` provides an explicit comparison mode. `--qb-bias-mode frozen` retains the current pending QB bias while expert and router weights continue updating; adaptive QB remains the default. Numerical CPU regressions cover stacked-versus-stage-local updates and both QB state transitions.

The historical 48-layer, 65K synthetic diagnostic ran on 192 H100s with BF16-stored parameters and per-expert normalization. Its PP24/EP8/CP1 layout placed two layers in each stage and kept expert traffic within eight-GPU workers. It was chosen to establish capacity; no matched PP8/EP32/CP4 Megatron comparison was performed. The README records the later CP2 result and the differences in batch size and attention helpers. Historical hardware results do not validate the new normalization or frozen-QB option, and no SFT/RL quality comparison has been run.

The affected safe suite passed 2,391 tests with four skips and five expected failures. Focused CPU checks passed 86 tests with one skip; required lint, full type checking, strict docs and source links passed.

#9662 is stacked above this foundation and adds checkpoint/data support, the GB200 launcher, tracked runtime setup and bounded main-recipe hardware validation. Before merge, this foundation still owns replacing the positional result from `initialize_stage_local_pipeline_state`, centralizing the repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers, and separating the synthetic runner lifecycle in `pipeline_smoke.main`. These deferred changes require compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation; #9662 then owns adapting its added checkpoint/data lifecycle.

topics.title: [RL] Add async Megatron launcher and score-centering study
topics.body:
Add a fully asynchronous Megatron/vLLM launcher for Snowball and Qwen, pinned to [MarinSkyRL #700](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/700). The launcher makes training, generation, evaluation, topology, context budget, checkpoint source, and artifact settings explicit. Score centering remains disabled by default.

The [study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/goal/score-centering-launcher-01a0bb6f/experiments/post_training/score_centering_study.md) retains exact rendered configs, response-level scores, repeated evaluations, W&B histories, consumed-prompt trackers, Iris task costs, runtime failures, and quality curves against updates, loss tokens, elapsed time, and H100-hours. A matched-token A/B/C probe separates inference-versus-trainer engine mismatch from stale-weight drift. The signed terms partly cancel, so a stable aggregate magnitude does not show that stale-weight drift is negligible.

At the measured Qwen incumbent (TIS cap 1.05, top-k 32, token-weighted mean consumed age about 4.7 updates), the three exploratory seed pairs favored score centering by +36.5, +43.5, and +9 answers out of 756. Three prespecified confirmation pairs gave +28.5, -23.5, and -5.5. The confirmation mean is -0.2 answers with a paired 95% Student-t interval of -65.8 to +65.4; the six-seed descriptive mean is +14.8 (-12.6 to +42.1). The initial signal did not replicate consistently. Matched exposure, loss tokens, elapsed time, and cost show no compute saving at this setting. Because no acceptable quality-loss margin was selected, the result does not establish non-inferiority.

The format-fixed Snowball pair completed nine updates per arm with active TIS and finite score centering. Six evaluations of the same step-five weights varied more than the small arm difference: completed-answer endpoint differences ranged from -33 to +11 out of 756, while baseline-adjusted differences ranged from -20 to +24. The original 4,096-token run completed updates six through nine, then failed during update ten. Five matched continuations restored the arm-specific step-five checkpoints with response caps from 3,840 down to 1,536 tokens, but each failed before completing resumed update six in TransformerEngine's unfused attention path. The configs requested FlashAttention; retained runtime logs show that installed FlashAttention 2.8.4 was outside the supported range through 2.8.3, so the runtime fell back to unfused attention. This report therefore makes no Snowball quality claim past step five.

Round-two diagnostics, Qwen confirmation, Snowball qualification, retries, generation, evaluation, and discarded work consumed 1,072.548303 reserved H100 task-hours. The measured evidence supports keeping score centering off by default in the tested Qwen range. Further Snowball training requires a runtime or backend change, or a severe response-length reduction that would materially change the experiment. A compatible FlashAttention attempt must first verify that the fused backend is active.

The final High-tier goal review found no implementation correctness defect. Its two completion blockers, omitted diagnostic task costs and missing clean-pair YAMLs, are fixed in `928887f72d`. Targeted launcher and cost tests pass. CI is running on that final review-fix commit.

topics.title: [vllm histograms] Store and query cumulative family snapshots
topics.body:
Store cumulative histograms as one record per engine and family and query them alongside scalar history. Disjoint integer bucket counts and floating-point bounds use existing `kind=histogram` records and the nullable `body_json` column. Scalar histogram observations and the scalar snapshot publisher retain their behavior. No new record kind, table, column, data backfill, or schema migration is needed.

The detailed and compact dashboard queries share histogram component normalization, publication validation, and delta calculation. A scalar publication supplies a baseline only when count, sum, and all bucket bounds known at that publication are present. Scalar counts at or above 2^53 are unavailable because their floating-point representation cannot guarantee exact source integers. Both queries reject conflicting copies and negative interval-bin counts. Identified scalar publications use their final component timestamp for query-window selection; untagged scalar publications must fit wholly within the window. The compact summary reads bucket rows for legacy scalar histograms and per-bin arrays for structured histograms. Epoch and sequence must either both be supplied or both be absent; an absent pair uses collection time as publication identity. The three-minute lookback retains duplicate copies for validation before selecting baselines. Structured buckets use one cumulative prefix sum. Equivalent numeric bucket spellings share a canonical label; integral labels render without `.0`. The dashboard withholds percentile and distribution estimates when a family has multiple bucket-bound schemas, including across scalar and structured publications. Client bounds are validated as 64-bit floating-point numbers, matching the server. Structured counts from 0 through 2^63-1 are supported; larger source counts are reported as publication loss.

In September 23–24, 2026 local measurements, a 32-engine, eight-family publication persisted 832 structured versus 6,208 scalar vLLM data rows and used 2 versus 8 HTTP POSTs. Row counts include histograms, gauges, and counters. A four-engine, three-hour replay reduced ingest time from 180.17 to 33.50 seconds. Its 30-minute detailed query preserved time-to-first-token mean and p50/p90/p99, with higher structured client peak RSS (474 versus 441 MB). A separate 32-engine, two-minute replay preserved output-length and time-per-output-token means, counts, and percentiles, plus all output-length bins. These historical single-job measurements do not establish current-head performance or the seven-day, 50-job overview query's 10-second target. The vLLM overview rejects results with more than one million input samples.

The root development lock uses DuckDB 1.5.4, matching the Grafana package lock for the new bucket expansion. Regional Finelog schemas, external histogram SQL consumers, and the released Rigging publisher in MarinSkyRL's frozen environment require verification before rollout. Part of #9382.
