The PR adds checkpoint merging, calibration, and exports that preserve the original base checkpoint (Base) layout. One localized correctness fix is needed before merge; the other findings are code consolidation.

**Blockers**

1. [experiments/weight_merging/constrained_merge.py:81](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3b775b18812fff9a746eb544fbdcf39b6feae2f9/experiments/weight_merging/constrained_merge.py#L81): Rejected exports remain usable as merge sources. The checkpoint is written before the final change-cap check and external audit; `CheckpointReader` only checks the historical `merge-recipe.json`/manifest convention, and constrained exports never create `merge-recipe.json`. A local probe changed two of eight scalars—25%, exceeding its 10% change cap—and raised without writing an audit. The rejected output still opened and became a donor for a completed merge. Create a temporary incomplete marker before export, reject marked directories in `CheckpointReader`, and remove the marker only after the change-cap check and successful external audit write. Share that finalization across the constrained, calibrated, and serial paths. Successful exports can still retain exactly Base's original files.

**Should fix**

2. [experiments/weight_merging/campaign_calibration_runtime.py:22](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3b775b18812fff9a746eb544fbdcf39b6feae2f9/experiments/weight_merging/campaign_calibration_runtime.py#L22): Dependency installation, SkyRL checkout, environment construction, and execution duplicate `calibration_runtime.py:20`. Changes to pins or checkout behavior must be maintained twice. Use one runtime entrypoint that selects the calibration module and applies the explicit SkyRL patch when supplied. Both launchers also create a checkout with `mkdtemp` and replace themselves with `execve`, leaving no cleanup path; run the child inside a `TemporaryDirectory` context with `subprocess.run(..., check=True)`.

3. [experiments/weight_merging/constrained_coefficients.py:62](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3b775b18812fff9a746eb544fbdcf39b6feae2f9/experiments/weight_merging/constrained_coefficients.py#L62): The chunk-budget allocation loop duplicates `calibrate.py:91`, with different tie handling. Keep each trainer's score calculation, but share a pure `allocate_chunk_counts(scores, limits, budget)` function whose ties follow insertion order in `scores`; each caller should supply its current tie ordering. This removes the repeated allocation loops without changing the calibration objectives.

**Tests to drop**

None.

**Related PRs**

No changed-path overlaps among the 100 open PRs queried.

All 46 focused CPU tests passed at this head. The completion failure was reproduced with local synthetic checkpoints. GPU calibration and full model merges were not run.

Successful finalization removes the output's temporary marker, preserving the original input checkpoint's file inventory.

Lint and type checks pass, along with 52 focused CPU tests and the broader safe suite (2,899 passed, five skipped, five xfailed). GPU calibration and full model merges were not run. CI is checking the pushed commit.

topics.title: [Post-training][Model merging] Initial Experiments in Model Merging with Snowball 67B A2B
topics.body:
We implemented eleven model-merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 Snowball 67B A2B checkpoint variants with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores. Sequential merging via selective expert transfer retained almost all of the NUPA source's performance and matched the BFCL source's score, but the three best merges retained essentially none of the Base model's routed experts. We have not yet run the complete cohort of policy evals needed to judge non-targeted performance.

[Earlier RLVR experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735) showed that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can strongly and unpredictably affect non-targeted benchmarks. It can introduce or repair behavioral defects that change scores while leaving the model's underlying “knowledge” essentially untouched. For example, a model might return every numeric answer, such as “31.7,” as “final_answer.31.7” instead of the requested “Final Answer: 31.7,” collapsing a benchmark score. We conservatively treat these as model defects to remedy under normal use conditions rather than grader defects to smooth. Each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats, so we investigated efficient ways to combine checkpoints.

Model merging is popular among hobbyists and is rumored to be used extensively at frontier labs, though the scientific literature is thin. Most merging methods use very few FLOPs and often require no GPUs. This makes merging relevant to our goal of reaching the frontier quickly and FLOP-efficiently.

The target Snowball checkpoint had largely improved but acquired two severe behavioral defects that sharply reduced NUPA and BFCL performance. We used two other Snowball models as merge sources. Each was an expert on one target benchmark, but both were generally inferior to the target, or Base, model. The objective was to raise performance on both disparate target benchmarks without degrading non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all standard merging approaches we tried failed to raise both target scores strongly. They restored capability weakly on both benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. Extensive experimentation led us to try sequential merging via selective expert transfer. It retained performance on both targets, but required discarding essentially all Base parameters from the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

These three merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched the source BFCL score. None appears to meet the objective of avoiding degradation on non-targeted benchmarks; we will reserve judgment until the complete policy eval cohort has run.

Sequential merging via selective expert transfer appears promising for complex MoE merges. Our best strategy combined weights from the NUPA, BFCL, and Base models:

1. Start with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template.
2. Replace selected NUPA routed experts with BFCL experts. In each layer, select 32 expert positions using BFCL activation measurements and copy BFCL weights into them. This discards all Base routed experts.
3. Change NUPA's shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We made three versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

The percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version had the highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model:

- Starting with BFCL, copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts yielded only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA, copying 32 BFCL-selected experts yielded 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor, the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We found no better joint result with those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights, and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce. This was likely an unusually difficult merge target because tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently:

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA's tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base's tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers. This affects benchmarks even with unchanged weights: the same input text can produce different token IDs, and the same output token ID can decode to different text. The numerical vocabulary did not change. Both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

The chat templates also formatted tool use differently:

- NUPA's template presents tool definitions as one JSON array; Base's presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA's template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided; Base's omits those IDs.
- The templates differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Using the other template changes the model input and therefore the benchmarks. In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input:

| Model weights | With Base configuration and tokenizer | With NUPA configuration and tokenizer |
|---|---:|---:|
| NUPA, with no expert transfer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 17.07% BFCL-Parity |
| NUPA, with 16 BFCL experts per layer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 21.14% BFCL-Parity |

In another ablation, restoring NUPA's own special-token rows increased NUPA200 from 29.00% to 39.00%. These rows represent control tokens, such as message boundaries.

The agent's experimental design was flawed and needs a follow-up study. It drifted almost immediately from adding specialist capabilities to Base toward combining the two specialists. We will enforce that specialist changes target only a small, measured fraction of Base weights in the follow-up study, and may also control for the tokenizer confound.

---

🤖

## Campaign 4 follow-up: constrained routed-expert transfer

### TL;DR

Campaign 4 tested 71 audited merges that transfer routed-expert rows from Reference-KL Step20 into Antidoom Step12. All 355 fixed-policy evaluation records completed. `adaptive-delta-08` led with a **220.40** four-target sum versus Base's **174.90**, while changing **9.47%** of Base's scalar weights. Its scores were 83.54 HumanEval+, 74.07 MBPP+, 34.33 OlympiadBench, and 28.46 BFCL-Parity; MATH500 was 93.60 versus Base's 95.00.

The top three candidates all used layer-adaptive donor deltas with coefficients above 1.0. Exact donor-row transfer did not match them: the best wide-support serial merge reached 204.66 while changing 27.77% of Base. The result supports selective, task-weighted delta extrapolation for this parent pair. It does not establish broad retention: the four transfer benchmarks selected the checkpoints, MATH500 was the only regression canary, and all scores are single runs.

### Public checkpoints

1. [`adaptive-delta-08` — Target Sum 220.40](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Adaptive-Delta-08-2026.10.14/tree/2fb31748eed37435c7472e80f81f34e306b2fa7a), revision `2fb31748eed37435c7472e80f81f34e306b2fa7a`
2. [`adaptive-delta-05` — Target Sum 213.49](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Adaptive-Delta-05-2026.10.14/tree/4a19865c0ed69efab0bf457804d2d698fb3f72f5), revision `4a19865c0ed69efab0bf457804d2d698fb3f72f5`
3. [`adaptive-delta-06` — Target Sum 213.48](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Adaptive-Delta-06-2026.10.14/tree/337eb566795323f93ee16bbf294da6efd5e48539), revision `337eb566795323f93ee16bbf294da6efd5e48539`

Each repository contains the evaluated weights, OpenMDW 1.1 license, exact recipe, original-Base readback audit, protocol, final tracker, and sanitized copies of the five sealed evaluation records. The repositories are public and ungated; the links above pin immutable revisions.

### Experiment design

Base was [Antidoom RLVR1 Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02/tree/50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e). The extraction target was [Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04/tree/fd07ef0f2b78a83099a0042e59c00de986e7b647). The selection objective was the unweighted percentage-point sum of HumanEval+, MBPP+, OlympiadBench, and BFCL-Parity. MATH500 was a regression canary and did not enter selection.

A merge could change at most 30.00% of Base's indexed scalar weights. Only rows of routed-expert gate, up, and down projection tensors were eligible. Every other weight and every non-weight file had to remain byte-for-byte identical to Base. Serial stages were measured against original Base, so an intermediate checkpoint could not reset the budget. The full public protocol is [here](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Adaptive-Delta-08-2026.10.14/blob/2fb31748eed37435c7472e80f81f34e306b2fa7a/provenance/campaign4/PROTOCOL.md).

The campaign covered eight method families: DARE-linear; serial DARE-TIES followed by ISO; targeted serial transfer; task-paired serial transfer; exact task-union transfer; layer-adaptive delta transfer; behavioral-residual grafting; and wide-support serial transfer. The initial 20 candidates reused Campaign 2's seed-0 R25 routed-expert support. Later candidates used fixed BFCL, HumanEval+, and MBPP+ routed-expert rankings. Construction wrote a temporary incomplete marker, materialized the candidate, read every stored object back, checked the support and actual-change limits, verified unchanged bytes outside support and across non-weight files, wrote and reread the external audit, then removed the marker.

Evaluation used the pinned October 2026 Marin policy: Marin `aaf1878ce65a1a05b386aef257b952fa7205283a`, Evalchemy `958cdb8019b7a4c8432fe85eb9572538ceb75950`, and Harbor `2203bacd03d82e9d4f2a9422f0b3f7e9bb7952cc`. Each candidate used one eight-H100 vLLM server shared by its five evaluations. The suites contained 164 HumanEval+ tasks, 378 MBPP+ tasks, 30 OlympiadBench tasks, 123 BFCL-Parity trials, and 500 MATH500 tasks. A score sealed only when at least 90% of declared trials were scoreable.

The implementation and reproduction guide are in [PR #10135](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10135). Run the merge commands from the immutable [Campaign 4 implementation revision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/a34255b3ad07099bccb13b5e4ace71a209d1c67f). Exact public replay artifacts are available for the three published checkpoints. For the remaining 68 candidates, the tracker publishes scores and recipe summaries; exact recipes and sealed record contents are not public, so exact byte-for-byte replay of the full search is not possible from public artifacts alone.

### Results

`adaptive-delta-08` recovered 64.08% of the extraction target's aggregate improvement over Base. By benchmark, it recovered 78.12% of the HumanEval+ gap, 84.40% of the MBPP+ gap, 44.98% of the OlympiadBench gap, and 59.57% of the BFCL-Parity gap. MATH500 fell 1.40 points.

The search showed three useful patterns:

- Exact transfer did not improve monotonically with breadth. Exact-union family scores ranged from 188.64 to 200.65; wide serial scores ranged from 195.64 to 204.66 while changing 20.19%–27.81% of Base. Interference at wider supports is one plausible explanation, but this sweep does not isolate its cause.
- Task-specific support was useful, but serially composing exact supports did not add their gains reliably. The best task-paired result was 198.60, and the best targeted serial result was 198.73.
- Layer-adaptive scaling produced the only candidates above 207.77. Its top three changed 8.18%–9.47% of Base, less than half the changed fraction of the widest exact transfers.

These comparisons are retrospective maxima from unequal family sizes. They isolate useful construction patterns for this parent pair; they do not estimate statistical uncertainty or performance on unmeasured tasks.

### Complete tracker

Scores are percentages. Target Sum is HumanEval+ + MBPP+ + OlympiadBench + BFCL-Parity using unrounded component scores. Merge time includes checkpoint construction and the original-Base readback audit. The tracker abbreviates the `bfclparity-pi` suite as BFCL-Parity.

topics.title: [Post-training] Explore capability-preserving model merging
topics.body:
TL;DR: Model merging is a promising direction for Marin: different Grug/Snowball checkpoints have complementary strengths, but we do not yet have a reliable way to combine them while preserving the base model's other capabilities. Cheap weight-space operations could make this orders of magnitude less expensive than on-policy distillation (OPD). We would benefit from expert input on how to make that tradeoff work for our mixture-of-experts (MoE) models.

The policy evaluation tracker illustrates the problem (percentages; higher is better):

| Checkpoint | MATH500 | GPQA-Diamond | HumanEval+ | NUPA | BFCL-Parity/Pi |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [Grug Antidoom Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02) | 95.00 | 67.30 | 72.60 | 0.10 | 5.70 |
| [Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92) | 89.60 | 42.90 | 68.90 | 40.60 | 16.30 |
| [Grug Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04) | 92.60 | 63.00 | 86.60 | 0.30 | 43.90 |

Source: [policy-tracker snapshot](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/inputs/TRACKER.md). These are policy NUPA scores; the merge study instead optimized NUPA200, a 200-task subset of the policy’s 5,000-task panel. BFCL-Parity/Pi is the policy's tool-use evaluation with the Pi agent. No checkpoint in this comparison achieves the best score in every column.

Our [initial study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975) shows both the appeal and the unresolved problem. Static merge construction typically required roughly 1e11–1e12 estimated arithmetic FLOPs per checkpoint, often without GPUs. This supports the prospect of a large compute advantage over OPD, which requires rollout generation and training; we have not run a matched OPD cost comparison. Evaluation and any calibration or expert-selection work add costs beyond static construction.

The best merge scored 36.50% on NUPA200 and 48.78% on BFCL-Parity, versus historical specialist references of 38.00% and 43.90%, respectively. But its recipe copied only 0.76% of all parameter values unchanged from the intended Base (Step12). On non-target benchmarks, it scored 89.80% MATH500 and 52.19% GPQA-Diamond, versus Base’s historical policy scores of 95.00% and 67.30%; these were not matched reruns. That study did not establish capability-preserving transfer into Base.

We would welcome advice from people with model-merging experience, especially on transferring specialist behavior into an existing MoE checkpoint with limited weight changes, handling expert/router compatibility and the tokenizer differences observed in #9975, and choosing retention evaluations that expose damage outside the target benchmarks.

Done when: expert feedback informs a concrete follow-up design with a fixed Base, explicit limits on weight changes, and pre-agreed target and non-target evaluation criteria.

topics.title: [analysis] Independent pre-registered forecast of the hero's final loss, with 80/95% intervals
topics.body: Hi @ClassicLarry @dlwh, To add uncertainty to the Aug 19 pre-registration in #8435, I made an independent forecast of the hero's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` (4K eval packing). It is frozen at 58% of training and uses only public data. **Result:** median **2.035**, 80% interval [2.023, 2.047], 95% [2.016, 2.054]. The Aug 19 pre-registration (2.039) sits at our 68th percentile, so the run looks on track for it. A finish near 2.10 looks very unlikely. **Method in brief** - The ladder is used only for the remaining drop from now to the end. The level comes from the hero's own post-swap evals, which makes the forecast nearly independent of the floor E. - Backtests set the drift persistence, the method error and an allowance for distance-dependent bias. They use held-out ladder rungs and the 67B-A2B run (#6044). In nested leave-one-out, the 80% intervals cover 14–15 of 16 held-out cases. - PTB gets its own term because of its noise and the exposures in #9874. A PTB-free companion target is forecast too: 2.047 [2.036, 2.059]. **One finding:** most of the 2.04 vs 2.10 gap comes from counting lm_head FLOPs in compute. On the H100 d768–d1536 runs, excluding them moves the fitted floor from 1.913 to 1.573 and the forecast from 2.116 to 2.037 (see the comment below for the refit's exact setting). **Pre-registration, code and scoring rules:** https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/prereg-v2-2026-10-09/preregistration_v2.md - The scoring rules were fixed in advance, including what happens if the context or the schedule changes. - This is v2. I revised v1 (median 2.045) the same day after re-auditing its backtests, on the same data. Both versions are tagged, and every change is listed. - I'll post a check-in at 70% and the scored comparison after the run ends.

topics.title: [levanter] Fix reverse slices of sharded flat fields
topics.body: Negative-step slices of sharded cache flat fields returned empty arrays because the reader requested a zero-length forward span. Read the covered span in forward order, then apply the negative stride. Reverse slices now return values across shard boundaries.

This one builds a second expert in a different domain and asks whether both experts' gains can be moved into B at once, and what it costs in the other domain (forgetting) and on unrelated benchmarks (collapse). Intervals that include 0 do not establish equivalence. - **Plain mixed SFT** is below RS-SFT by 5.8 [3.5, 8.2] on the MMLU-Pro subset and below E on CruxEval input. - **Merging** at half strength beats B in both domains with no training but stays 8–10 pp below the trained arms on CruxEval output; at full strength it regresses badly on GSM8K and GPQA-D with runaway generations. - **Collapse checks**: GSM8K at or above B for every trained arm; MATH500 and GPQA-D at or above B on the RS-SFT and MOPD finals (RS-SFT's GPQA-D 57.6 is +15.7 [+10.4, +21.0] over B, one evaluation, reported without interpretation); IFEval 1–3 pp below B (RS −2.8 [−5.2, −0.2], MOPD −1.1 [−3.6, +1.2]). ## Reading Two experts can be moved into B at once: both RS-SFT and MOPD improve both domains over B and land at or above each expert in that expert's domain on the point estimates. The two methods trade off by domain and are not matched controls for each other (RS-SFT had verifier access, 8 teacher samples per prompt and a different token budget; MOPD cost 6× more H100-hours). Plain SFT recovers less; merging is a cheap partial substitute at half strength only. ## Caveats - One evaluation pass per checkpoint except the stated repeats; plain SFT's 803-vs-603 selection used two passes each. Intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons or checkpoint selection. - Both primary targets are test-exposed (training-is-test); the held-out MMLU-Pro questions are an additional probe, never a selection input. - The RS-SFT demo selector used an older answer-extraction rule than the evaluator: 14 of its 1,400 MMLU-Pro demos are wrong under the evaluator's rule, 15 prompts would have been gained and 1 lost, 45 would have used a different sample. topics.title: [eval] Preserve completed evaluation results on Iris retries
topics.body:
Iris retries now reuse an existing successful record before starting model serving. Conditional record publication preserves the first success when a retry later fails or concurrent attempts race. The Evalchemy child reads a FineStore completion marker and runs without a local output directory. This covers the record-to-StepSpec success gap described in #9813.

This draft cannot merge until marin-community/evalchemy publishes FineStore-backed request resume and completion markers, then Marin updates its Evalchemy pin. The affected Marin suite passed 334 tests, and the fork's FineStore and resume suite passed 113 tests with four skipped. Conditional publication was exercised locally; S3 and GCS were not exercised here.

topics.title: [skills] Check an eval step on one rack before a hero cutover
topics.body:
Add a preflight item to the hero cutover checklist: a one-rack run of the deploy commit restores the handoff and trains through a dropless eval and the steps after it. The 200-step trial usually ends before the new run's first eval, so a cutover can go live without ever switching between its eval and train executables, and that switch has failed before (#8861).

Also note that the public hero report starts each phase's curves at the run's `report_phase_start` config value. The 2026-10-09 handoff to `hero-mfu30-step231k` showed its whole inherited history until the value was set.

topics.title: [iris] Sandbox pods cannot pull task images from envreg on CoreWeave or GCP
topics.body:
Sandbox pods created by shellbox's Iris backend cannot pull images from the task registry `envreg.208261-marin-gpu.coreweave.app`, on CoreWeave as well as on GCP.

Observed on `cw-rno2a` with a gVisor sandbox for `envreg.208261-marin-gpu.coreweave.app/capability-infra/taskforge-grader-base@sha256:63eb0b5c3efb5b2e3def1e81f9e076a4c62a077ad5f631cfef95ea9f441240b3` (a public-content image published by `skopeo copy` with the `capability-registry-publisher` credential): `ImagePullBackOff`, then the 600 s sandbox timeout, then the grader timed out. The same sandbox with `python:3.12-slim` was ready in 20 s and graded. Earlier probes on the GCP workers failed the same way ("workers cannot pull from envreg", recorded on the Taskforge side since 2026-10-05).

Task generation and curation publish every task image and the grader image to envreg by digest, so every image-backed task and every script-graded task is unrunnable on Iris until sandbox pods carry a pull credential for that registry, or the images are mirrored to a registry the clusters already pull from.

Asks: (1) a cluster-wide image pull secret for envreg on the sandbox pod spec (all Iris clusters, both providers), or guidance on which registry Taskforge should publish to instead; (2) the registry speaks only Basic auth (`WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="envgen"`), so if a scoped read-only credential is preferred it has to be created on the registry side.

comments.body: 🤖 As of 2026-10-14 the task registry (envreg.208261-marin-gpu.coreweave.app) serves GET/HEAD anonymously with Basic auth kept on writes at the Traefik ingress, so sandbox pods need no pull secret for it; a cold pull from a cw-rno2a sandbox is still to be exercised, and the change is recorded in capability_env_gen-dev/docs/image_registry.md with a rollback.

🤖 Node-side pull confirmed on cw-rno2a: an Iris job with task image envreg.208261-marin-gpu.coreweave.app/capability-infra/oci-smoke@sha256:b7f3d86d6e84fc17718c48bcde1450807faa2d56704205c697b4bd5df7b9e29f under the sandbox container profile pulled with no credential and reached RUNNING, so envreg no longer needs the pull secret this issue asks for; cw-us-east-02a was not tested.

topics.title: [iris] Cached job env reaches child jobs after the job scrubs its secrets
topics.body:
Iris caches a job's environment before the job's own code runs, so a job that scrubs secrets from `os.environ` and `IRIS_JOB_ENV` at startup still hands the unscrubbed environment to any non-sandbox child job it launches.

Observed on `cw-us-east-02a` during a Zephyr feasibility spike for Taskforge: the Taskforge queue job removes `GLM_API_TOKEN`, `WANDB_API_KEY` and the other host secrets from its environment at start (`scrub_child_environment`), and afterwards both `os.environ` and `IRIS_JOB_ENV` are clean. The job environment Iris had already cached still held `GLM_API_TOKEN` and `WANDB_API_KEY`, so a non-sandbox child job would inherit them. Sandbox children (ShellSim, bwrap, gVisor) received no env in this run; gVisor sandboxes did see the `IRIS_*` variables and the Kubernetes service addresses, including the controller's.

Asks: (1) a documented way for a job to launch children with an explicit environment that does not include the parent's cached env (an allowlist on the child job spec, or a per-submission `inherit_env=False`); (2) sandbox pods should not receive `IRIS_*` variables or the controller's service address unless the submitter asks for them, since model-controlled code runs there.

Related earlier notes on the Taskforge side: CoreWeave `task_env` injecting object-store keys into pods (not reproduced on `cw-rno2a` in this spike) and child jobs inheriting a parent's explicit `-e` secrets.

Original description ~~~markdown This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved. At d768–d1280 each layer is recomputed. At d1280 the attention branch is also rematerialized. - The model keeps one layer stack per mixer kind. **Optimizer** | Group | Update rule | LR | Parameters | |---|---|---|---| | `muonh` | MuonH | MuonH LR | all attention and MoE matrices: MLA `W_q`/`W_dkv`/`W_uk`/`W_uv`/`W_o`; KDA `W_q`/`W_k`/`W_v`/`W_o`/`W_g`; experts; shared experts; latent down/up. Each matrix's norm stays fixed at its init value. - **AdamH:** the Adam direction with the same Frobenius-sphere (hyperball) projection. - **Adam:** β1 0.9. Only the router and the attention output gate get decoupled weight decay (0.02). No other parameter gets weight decay, and there's no gradient clipping. - **Schedule:** 1% warmup, then linear decay to 0.05× peak. - **Peak values** from `MoeHeuristic` (they depend on tokens, width and batch): - Adam LR = `0.0876 · tokens^−0.346 · D^−0.345 · √(tokens per batch)`. - MuonH LR = 13/3 × Adam LR. - β2 = `0.999^(tokens per batch / 131072)`. - ε = `9.68e−18 · √(steps)`. - At d512 with 2384 steps: MuonH LR 0.0227, Adam LR 0.0052, β2 0.996, ε 4.7e−16. The agent picks up new comments at its next batch. The main goal of a single experiment should be to learn about the system. This means that if you tweak one knob and the loss goes off the rails, the experiment can still be considered a success! We better understand the system sensitivity! Building knowledge through failed experiments will bring us closer to the long term goal of better models. ## For the agent - Read `experiments/grug/fast_track/README.md` and `agent.md` first. MSAR gives each gate m queries ("streams"): - **Stream 0** reads the sources as they are, exactly like today. - **Streams r ≥ 1** first pass every source through its own causal depthwise convolution along the sequence (kernels 4/8/12, zero-init, never crossing document boundaries), then attend over those. - **Mixer:** a small sigmoid mixer, `sigmoid(α·RMSNorm(concat z)·W + b)`, weights the m reads into the sublayer's input. - **Final gate:** the one before the LM head stays single-stream. **Code:** `attn_res_streams` / `attn_res_stream_kernels` / `attn_res_stream_mixer`, default off; with m=1 the model is bit-identical to today. The mixer's W and everything else stay normal. A fix is in progress, then m4/m2 rerun. **Update 2: mixer arms rerun at [`912bd13876`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/912bd13876).** - **The NaN was an XLA GPU miscompile.** On 8 GPUs, the bf16 gradients of the tiny mixer α `[2]` and b `[2, m]` leaves come out of the combined float32 gradient all-reduce through a *bitcast* instead of a convert, so the leaves receive raw float32 bit-halves. Keeping those two leaves float32 at compute fixes it; the corrupted runs were rerun under new ids (`m4b`, `m2b`). - **All three arms win at equal data by about −0.011 to −0.013**, which is 2–2.5× the noise threshold: - The mixer adds only about 0.0014 over the plain sum (m4 −0.0125 vs m4nomix −0.0111), inside the noise. - m=2 with a single kernel-4 stream (−0.0109) matches m=4. - **So the gain comes from the convolved streams, not the mixer or the stream count.** Next: a fixed-time run (MSAR costs about +18% step time), and controls for whether the gain is just longer temporal reach (`sconv_kernel` 8/12 on the existing write-side convs) or depends on the per-channel basis (scalar-tap streams). **Batch 2: finding the minimal version** ([`23bd387bcc`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/23bd387bcc)). evalchemy209.title: Make Evalchemy results and resume state FineStore native
evalchemy209.body:
Write evaluation aggregates, normalized samples, and request checkpoints directly to FineStore. Resume restores committed requests by default. Before generation, the evaluator validates the stored task list and each task's fingerprint, including all supplied generation overrides. It initializes the model before this validation. Results and samples enter the archive in one transaction, so a retry leaves a completed result unchanged. FineStore result writes use the same guarded SymPy serialization as the CLI display.

`--output_path` and `--finestore_output_path` select the same FineStore archive. Existing scripts keep `--output_path` and use distinct archive paths for distinct evaluations. Native JSON/JSONL result serialization, SQLite resume state, temporary output staging, and the unused TACC listener are removed. The TACC distributed batch scripts remain. The serve-and-eval runner and regression gate read the same archive; the gate keeps `--results` as its archive selector. Concurrent writers to one archive have not been exercised locally.

Part of marin-community/marin#9972. The Marin retry work is tracked in marin-community/marin#9813.
